📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Syam Sreeshylam.

Curving ceilings sweep down to frame the two small gardens that flank this home in Kerala, India, designed by local architecture studio Fictional Project.

Named Interstitial Living, the home in the village of Adoor was designed for a family of four who wanted to feel connected to the outside, in particular the lush greenery surrounding the site.

This led Fictional Project to pull the home’s built volume back to create space for two planted yards on either side, overlooked by the home’s pared-back and open interiors.

“The residence is careful not to overpower, becoming one with the landscape,” the studio told Dezeen.

Interstitial Living is organised around a bedroom at its centre, which is housed within a cubic volume finished in cement plaster.

A small window in this bedroom overlooks a potted tree within a cut-out in the floor of the adjacent living room, which faces the yard to the west through a row of full-height windows above a built-in timber bench.

On the opposite side of the home, the kitchen overlooks the eastern yard through a row of windows above its countertops. Both these spaces are defined by the curving white-plastered ceilings overhead, which sweep down from the centre of the home.

According to recent reports, “The scale of the residence allows for intimate working spaces in the kitchen and a welcoming living room, all accentuated by the dynamic nature of the roof. The other spaces negotiate the private/public nature of the indoors,” the studio explained.

“The concavity of the roof creates a visual connection to the outdoors, becoming a marker that emerges from within the site.”.

“It breaks the rigidity of a traditional sloping roof, helping create fluid indoor spaces. Nothing here is built or conceived in isolation, but rather as interconnected systems,” it added.

The smaller first floor contains a second bedroom, bathroom and a study area, which overlook the living space below from a steel-framed landing and internal windows.

While the internal finishes were kept minimal, the exterior of the home and its boundary walls were built using terracotta-toned textured blocks, which the studio described as introducing a sense of “groundedness and warmth”.

Other dwellings in Kerala recently featured on Dezeen include a home by InLe Architects framed and shaded by two large mango trees and a farmhouse by Evolving Radical Aesthetics that is built into a hillside above a carved-out, open-air temple.

Photography by Syam Sreeshylam.

Upcoming York studio SHoP Architects has released designs for a ribbed supertall skyscraper in Miami, announced alongside the launch of a luxury brand for which Serbian tennis player Novak Djokovic is developing amenity facilities.

SHoP Architects, who are behind some of Upcoming York City’s tallest buildings, designed the 1,049-foot-tall (320-metre-tall) skyscraper around ATMA, a luxury brand being released by hospitality operator Aman Group.

If completed at the stated height, it would be taller than the city’s current tallest skyscraper, and have the same projected height as the in-progress Waldorf Astoria Hotel & Residences Miami, which has been cited as the city’s future tallest.

It has been revealed that the skyscraper will include a hotel, residences and a members’ club. According to Aman Group, ATMA’s “advanced wellness programming and world-class sport facilities” will be developed “exclusively” with Djokovic, who is credited as a global partner of the fresh brand.

Designs for the skyscraper itself show a ribbed form of balconied terraces organised around a central void that runs from the crown to the podium.

It is planned for Miami’s Brickell neighbourhood, and Aman Group noted that the floor-to-ceiling windows of the skyscraper will merge the “futuristic architecture with the bay”.

Recent findings suggest that toronto-based interiors outfit Studio Paolo Ferrari has been chosen as the interiors lead on the project. It will include condos with one to five bedrooms, with six-bedroom penthouses pushed to the top of the skyscraper.

The structure will have setbacks at the upper floors, presumably to create more panoramic views for residences in the penthouses.

The ATMA concept is based around what Aman Group calls “performance-driven lifestyle”.

“Monolithic architecture meets biomorphic design, furniture is shaped naturally to the human form and ambience adjusts sensitively to residents’ and guests’ circadian rhythm,” stated Aman Group.

Djokovic’s programme, meanwhile, will include a 120,000-square-foot spa and wellness centre.

“ATMA Miami will sit at the pinnacle of what performance living can achieve,” mentioned Djokovic.

OKO Group and Oak Row Equities were declared as developers for the project.

SHoP Architects is no stranger to supertall luxury residences. It designed New York’s skinniest supertall skyscraper to have single-floor apartments on the city’s so-called Billionaires Row. It also designed the Brooklyn Tower, the tallest structure in the borough.

Images courtesy of Aman Group.

📅 15 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1071 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that temperatures are starting to rise, with some parts of the US facing a record-setting early heat wave this week.
  • That’s the major takeaway from fresh research published in the journal Neurology: The study uncovered three lesser-known factors that can trigger migraine—and these triggers can crop up even more in the late spring and summer.
  • If you’re one of the 12% of Americans who deals with these headaches, this is information to keep in your back pocket.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that temperatures are starting to rise, with some parts of the US facing a record-setting early heat wave this week. But while you’re probably focused on staying cool, there’s one more thing that should be on your radar: a higher-than-usual risk of migraine headaches.

That’s the major takeaway from fresh research published in the journal Neurology: The study uncovered three lesser-known factors that can trigger migraine—and these triggers can crop up even more in the late spring and summer.

If you’re one of the 12% of Americans who deals with these headaches, this is information to keep in your back pocket. Here’s what the study found, plus how doctors who treat patients with migraine recommend protecting yourself.

According to recent reports, for the study, researchers followed 7,032 people living in Israel for about a decade who suffered from migraines. During the study period, researchers looked at participants’ daily exposure to air pollution, along with tracking weather conditions. They also looked at how often and when people visited the hospital or their primary care doctor with a migraine. That data was compared to the levels of pollution and weather conditions on that particular day, along with seven days before that.

Recent findings suggest that during the study period, 2,215 people (or 32%) had at least one visit to the hospital or a clinic with a migraine. The researchers also found that 47% of participants in the study bought triptan medications at one point or another—fast-acting prescription medications that are designed to stop a migraine—with most using at least two tablets a month.

Ultimately, the researchers discovered a link between three weather-related factors and migraine: air pollution, temperature (including UV exposure), and humidity. First, they found a correlation between higher levels of air pollution and the most number of visits to a hospital or clinic for a migraine. They also found that the day with the least visits to the hospital or clinic also had lower-than-average pollution levels. People with short-term exposure to high levels of nitrogen dioxide (a common pollutant from traffic exhaust) were 41% more likely to go to the hospital or clinic for migraine than people who weren’t exposed to high levels of the gas.

The study also revealed that people who were exposed to high levels of UV rays from the sun on a given day were 23% more likely to visit a healthcare provider for migraine symptoms than those who weren’t. High temperatures and low humidity appear to be linked to more migraine headaches, likely because they amplify the effect of nitrogen dioxide, the researchers said.

With climate change intensifying how often we deal with heat waves and pollution, it’s vital to consider these risk factors when it comes to migraine, the researchers wrote.

It’s vital to note that the study didn’t prove that air pollution, heat, and lower humidity levels cause migraines—it just found a link between them. But doctors say there’s likely something here.

Air pollution can spark neuroinflammation (the immune system’s inflammatory response in the brain and spinal cord), which is a risk factor for migraine, Sana Ghafoor, MD, neurologist at Tufts Medical Center, tells SELF. This may cause a release of pain chemicals like calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and substance P that can lead to a migraine, Dr. Ghafoor notes.

Recent findings suggest that air pollution may be particularly problematic for people with allergies who also struggle with migraines, Clifford Segil, DO, a neurologist at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, California, tells SELF. The body may see air pollution as an allergen and mount an immune response, which can spark a migraine in people who are sensitive to this trigger, he explains.

Then, there’s the fact that heat can impact blood vessels and nerves. “When people heat up, nerves and blood vessels in tight locations can become irritated, as the diameter of a blood vessel or nerves increases with heat,” Dr. Segil states. That, too, can trigger a migraine. You’re also more susceptible to getting dehydrated when it’s hot out, Dr. Ghafoor says: “If you're overheated and dehydrated, those can also trigger migraines.”.

It has been revealed that dr. Segil points out that high humidity common in the spring and summer (and not just that related to air pollution) can trigger migraines too. High humidity causes you to sweat and lose water, which can decrease the amount of blood in your blood vessels (if you don’t replace it), Dr. Segil states. “This decreases the diameter of blood vessels and can cause headaches, just like an increased blood vessel diameter,” he says.

Industry observers note that dr. Ghafoor states she often sees more patients have migraine headaches when high humidity strikes. “Even with small [atmospheric] pressure changes, it can activate nerve endings and sinuses, which can lead to the release of pain chemicals,” she says.

These are some of the most common migraine triggers, according to the US National Library of Medicine:.

These foods and ingredients can also trigger migraines, per the US National Library of Medicine:.

Migraine triggers are personal, making it notable to do what you can to figure out yours and then try to avoid them as best as possible. (Dr. Ghafoor recommends keeping a headache diary to try to narrow things down.) But factors like air pollution, heat, and humidity can be tough to avoid.

Industry observers note that if levels of air pollution are high in your area, Dr. Segil recommends wearing a face mask like an N95 when you need to be outdoors. Keeping your windows shut and running an air purifier can also help tamp down on pollution indoors. If you’d like, you can track pollution levels throughout the day and try to stay inside during peak times, Dr. Ghafoor indicates.

When heat and humidity strikes, Dr. Ghafoor recommends doing what you can to stay well hydrated. “Make sure that it’s not just water, but electrolytes too,” she claims. “All of that is a very crucial part of lifestyle management for patients who have migraine.”.

Sources indicate that ultimately, doing your best to try to figure out your triggers (and avoid them) can go a long way toward helping to keep you more comfortable on a regular basis. “Knowing and identifying migraine triggers is very important,” Dr. Ghafoor says. “It’s empowering the patient to understand their disease.”.

Collective housing fills the final section: the rental housing building in Málaga, winner of the Andalusia Architecture Award 2024, the 66 homes with terraces in Estepona and the Alborada residential building in Granada. The book closes with a small hotel at the foot of the Alhambra.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by James Brittain (unless stated otherwise).

Canadian studio Sid Lee Architecture has created a curved-glass hotel that takes cues from the burgeoning wine region of Ontario.

The Montreal-based studio recently unveiled The Clayfield Hotel, a 60-room hotel with a restaurant, ballroom and rooftop terrace in Niagara-on-the-Lake.

The rounded 94,000-square-foot (8,732-square metre) hotel sits on a property in the historic village that is being transformed by winemakers.

“The Clayfield was conceived as a upcoming hub for Niagara-on-the-Lake, a place where wine culture and hospitality find a home,” Martin Leblanc, architect and co-founding partner of Sid Lee Architecture, told Dezeen.

“Its layered contours, rounded geometry and rhythmic wood elements translate the surrounding vineyard landscape into a building that celebrates the region’s contribution to Canadian winemaking.”.

The hotel was conceived as a pavilion set in the emerging townscape between vineyards and the Clayfield Commons housing development on an agricultural road.

The curved form allows access and connection to its surroundings in multiple directions.

“The hotel acts as a threshold between these typologies, connecting the vineyard and the denser village-like development around it,” Leblanc noted.

“Its exterior wood elements recall the rhythm of the vine rows, the layered concrete refers to the clay soil and the reflective glass registers the changing light, sky and seasons.”.

The studio mentioned that the organic, natural flow of a hotel is essential to the lasting success of the design.

Working back and forth between the architecture and the interior design, the studio laid out spaces to progress from public to private and back again, integrating moments for visitors to discover the landscape.

In a recent development, “As visitors approach and circulate around the building, it frames changing views of the vines, the plaza and the emerging neighbourhood,” Leblanc mentioned. “The lobby acts as a gateway to the vineyard, while the rooftop terrace reconnects the hotel experience with its broader surroundings.”.

Meanwhile, the staircase acts as a connector, transition and centrepiece between the plaza, lobby and upper levels.

“Inside, we chose a palette that speaks to the natural beauty of Niagara’s wine country: walnut panelling, concrete, dark amaranth-coloured leather, greige limestone and woven fabrics,” Leblanc mentioned, calling out the limestone registration desk chiselled from the Niagara Escarpment and the restaurant’s curved bar that resembles the shape of the building.

With mostly Teknion furniture, each space represents a season of the vineyard, from spring in the lobby to winter in the guest rooms with more quiet, reserved furnishings that complete the rooms that fan out from the rounded concrete strata.

Founded in 2009, Sid Lee Architecture has six offices across North America and Europe. The studio previously remodelled its own offices in an I.M. Pei office building, overhauled the interiors of the iconic Fairmont Queen Elizabeth Hotel and created an artisan-inspired workplace for video game designers – all in Montreal.

#80044. After Losing My Son, I Didn't Want to Be ‘Strong’

📅 15 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1016 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

After Losing My Son, I Didn't Want to Be ‘Strong’

📅 15 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1016 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • During my pregnancy with my son Milan, I remember sitting with a pain that didn’t feel normal.
  • At the time of my pregnancy with Milan, I had already experienced a high-risk pregnancy and an emergency C-section during a previous pregnancy.
  • If someone with years of labor and delivery experience can recognize the signs, advocate for herself, and still be failed, what happens to the women with less information, fewer resources, or less confidence that they will be heard?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

During my pregnancy with my son Milan, I remember sitting with a pain that didn’t feel normal. It was sharp, persistent, and unsettling in a way I couldn’t ignore. As a former labor and delivery nurse, I understood the risks in a way many patients do not. I knew what to watch for. I knew my history. I knew when something felt wrong. Yet when I raised concerns, they were not met with the urgency they deserved.

At the time of my pregnancy with Milan, I had already experienced a high-risk pregnancy and an emergency C-section during a previous pregnancy. I knew that the vertical incision on my uterus could put a future pregnancy at risk. I spoke up. I asked questions. I paid attention to my body. Still, when I experienced a uterine rupture, I was navigating a system that did not respond with the level of care and urgency that the moment required.

If someone with years of labor and delivery experience can recognize the signs, advocate for herself, and still be failed, what happens to the women with less information, fewer resources, or less confidence that they will be heard?

Recent findings suggest that conversations during Black Maternal Health Week often center around one urgent truth: Black women are still far more likely to die from pregnancy-related causes in this country than white women. This is not an assumption. It is a proven fact, and it should stop all of us in our tracks. It also does not only impact one socioeconomic group. It affects everyone, including some of the most visible and resourced women in the world.

According to recent reports, as the founder of Mielle, my mission is to empower women, especially Black women, to express their authentic selves. At its core, that mission is about care, agency, and visibility, which is why conversations like this matter. It’s about showing up for every part of Black women’s experience. We need to talk more candidly about what happens to Black women who survive the trauma of miscarriage or stillbirth, and the prolonged mental health challenges that can follow, including postpartum depression.

Black women are expected to remain “strong” while navigating medical emergencies. We’re dismissed, told to wait, to calm down, and to trust a system that has not always earned that trust. We survive experiences that change our families and us forever. And then, too often, we are expected to do something just as impossible: keep going as if survival is the end of the story. It is not.

In a recent development, that is why Black Maternal Health Week cannot be about mortality alone. It must also be about what it means to live after trauma, preventable harm, and loss that reshapes your life.

In a recent development, the data make clear that this crisis is ongoing. Black women are about three times more likely to die from pregnancy-related causes than white women, and more than 80% of those deaths are considered preventable. Black infants also die at more than twice the rate of white infants. These are not random gaps. They reflect a healthcare system and a culture that too often normalizes Black women’s pain instead of responding to it.

Research shows that one in five women, or about 20%, report mistreatment during maternity care, but for Black women, that figure climbs to nearly 30%, reflecting more frequent experiences of bias, disrespect, and lack of autonomy in clinical settings. Nearly half of women say they have held back from asking questions or sharing concerns. In one of the most vulnerable moments of a person’s life, too many are already calculating whether speaking up will make things worse.

Recent findings suggest that in my own life, grief did not arrive quietly. It entered my marriage, my motherhood, my body, my faith, and eventually my work. In my book, The Glory In Your Story, I write about how grief does not follow a timeline. It becomes part of who you are, and healing begins not by outrunning it, but by acknowledging it.

Recent findings suggest that that matters because so many Black women are praised for being strong when what we actually need is space to be human. After losing Milan, I returned to work. I kept moving. I built Mielle. From the outside, it can look like a story of resilience. And in many ways, it is. But we have to be honest about the lessons we take from stories like mine.

According to recent reports, the lesson should not be that Black women are uniquely equipped to carry devastating grief and still perform at a high level. It should not be that our resilience makes systemic failures acceptable. And it should not be that we have to turn survival into something productive just to make our pain legible.

Too often, we celebrate the comeback without sitting long enough with the conditions that made it necessary.

Faith carried me. Purpose helped me rebuild. But none of that changes the reality that more listening, better care, stronger hospital systems, and greater urgency might have changed my story. If we are serious about maternal health, we have to be just as serious about saying that clearly.

Black Maternal Health Week gives us an opportunity to think more broadly about what justice looks like. It looks like hospitals are equipped for emergencies. It looks like providers who listen to Black women the first time, without requiring patients to fight to be believed. It looks like support for families after loss–not just during a crisis. And it looks like making space for grief without expecting Black women to turn it into inspiration before we are ready.

It has been revealed that it’s time that we honor not only the women we have lost, but also the women still here carrying what the system could not or would not hold for them. Survival is not the finish line. Being heard, protected, and cared for should be.

Tech Report: Cosentino supports architectural creativity with Ēclos mineral surface

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cosentino aims to put the creative freedom of architects and designers front and centre with its Ēclos surface, designed for three-dimensional compositions with refined edges, corners and waterfall ends.
  • Ēclos is the Spanish brand’s latest mineral surface material, made with advanced methods to emulate the look of natural stone and be free of crystalline silica.
  • The surface is made with Cosentino’s proprietary Inlayr manufacturing process, which makes the rich and naturalistic veining run through the slab.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cosentino aims to put the creative freedom of architects and designers front and centre with its Ēclos surface, designed for three-dimensional compositions with refined edges, corners and waterfall ends.

Ēclos is the Spanish brand’s latest mineral surface material, made with advanced methods to emulate the look of natural stone and be free of crystalline silica.

The surface is made with Cosentino’s proprietary Inlayr manufacturing process, which makes the rich and naturalistic veining run through the slab.

This gives Ēclos a premium look, Cosentino explained, and makes it a fitting constituent for the most sophisticated interiors.

According to Cosentino, it is in the junctions and details that a kitchen or room feels resolved and where its architectural character emerges.

“For architects and designers, the section deserves as much consideration as the elevation,” said the company. “The placement of a joint, the treatment of an edge and the relationship between adjoining surfaces shape how a material is perceived.”.

“These details establish the architectural language of an element, whether the intention is to suggest a continuous volume or to make its assembly visible.”.

Although surfaces are often selected based on their colour or pattern, Cosentino notes that full-body design should be just as crucial a consideration, allowing exposed edges and transitions between levels or materials to contribute to building a coherent form.

“With Ēclos, the patterning is constructed within the slab rather than confined to its face,” continued the brand. “That makes the relationship between surface and depth an notable part of the design conversation, particularly where edges remain visible.”.

“The interest lies not just in the appearance of the material, but in how it can be cut, assembled and brought into a project with adjacent finishes.”.

Its fabricators can advise how cutting, profiling, jointing and installation can help a designer’s vision come together.

The process can involve reviewing samples, fabrication drawings and, where appropriate, physical mock-ups.

“The position of a seam or the treatment of an exposed edge can subtly alter the proportions and perceived weight of an element,” said Cosentino.

“The aim is not necessarily to make every joint disappear, but to make each one deliberate.”.

“Whether the intention is a continuous volume or a clearly expressed assembly, the junction deserves as much consideration as the surface itself,” the brand continued.

Ēclos rolled out earlier this year and joins an expanding portfolio of low-silica, high-recycled mineral surface worktops from Cosentino, including Silestone, Dekton and Sensa.

It is suitable for both residential and commercial environments and can be used on worktops, splashbacks, walls and other surfaces.

The first Ēclos collection – Eclectic Veins – incorporates 10 stone-like designs, ranging from ice-white styles to dramatic darks, all made with a minimum of 50 per cent recycled content.

The material is practical for everyday use, withstanding scratches and stains, and is easy to clean and maintain.

It is also resistant to temperatures of up to 220 degrees Celsius, including contact with hot cookware.

To learn more about Cosentino and Ēclos, visit the tech giant’s website.

#80041. Obstructive Sleep Apnea Impacts Women Differently.

📅 16 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1710 w)

Obstructive Sleep Apnea Impacts Women Differently.

📅 16 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1710 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There are at least a dozen reasons why women may wake up with a headache, jitter with anxiety, or struggle to keep their eyes open at work, no matter how well they think they slept: menstruation, menopause, motherhood—the list truly goes on.
  • Industry observers note that if you immediately pictured an older man snoozing on a couch and snoring like a lawn mower, you’re not alone.
  • There’s still much to discover about the biology underlying these distinctions, but research suggests that hormonal fluctuations throughout life, differences in upper airway anatomy, and even social stigmas about how women should sleep are likely at play.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are at least a dozen reasons why women may wake up with a headache, jitter with anxiety, or struggle to keep their eyes open at work, no matter how well they think they slept: menstruation, menopause, motherhood—the list truly goes on. But these symptoms, as vague as they are, could actually stem from a health condition that’s historically been deemed a “male disease”: obstructive sleep apnea, or OSA.

Industry observers note that if you immediately pictured an older man snoozing on a couch and snoring like a lawn mower, you’re not alone. It wasn’t until the ’90s that researchers first recognized that OSA, which causes you to repeatedly stop breathing while asleep, often presents differently in women than it does in men. For starters women with the condition may not even snore.

There’s still much to discover about the biology underlying these distinctions, but research suggests that hormonal fluctuations throughout life, differences in upper airway anatomy, and even social stigmas about how women should sleep are likely at play.

“The disease itself was defined in men,” explains Jennifer Martin, PhD, a behavioral sleep medicine specialist and professor at Florida International University’s Herbert Wertheim College of Medicine in Miami. “The way men and women breathe when they’re asleep is not the same, and our definition of the disease doesn’t account for that.”.

It has been revealed that although obstructive sleep apnea appears to be less common and typically milder in women (at least before menopause), studies suggest that the consequences of the disease, if left untreated, can be similar, if not worse, for us, making it vital to learn the signs and seek help. Here’s what we know about obstructive sleep apnea and its impact on women. Plus, experts explain how to advocate for the best care if you think you may have the condition.

Sleep apnea is one of several conditions that fall under the sleep-disordered breathing umbrella. The most common type is OSA, which happens when your upper airway repeatedly collapses during sleep, making it harder for air to reach your lungs, says Anita Valanju Shelgikar, MD, a sleep medicine physician with University of Michigan Health and president of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

Recent findings suggest that the textbook symptoms of this condition—which, for the record, were determined based on studies mostly involving men—include loud snoring and dramatic gasps for air as a person tries to continue breathing while asleep. But this often isn’t the case for women, Dr. Shelgikar tells SELF. Instead, women with OSA are more likely to have nightmares, wake up multiple times a night, have trouble staying asleep, and deal with insomnia, which then causes symptoms like daytime fatigue, morning headaches, and mood swings. Women also have more hypopneas (shallow breaths with less oxygen flow), whereas men tend toward apneas (complete pauses in breathing).

Some experts speculate that it’s possible snoring isn’t commonly reported among women with this disorder because they’re embarrassed to talk about it, given society expects them to sleep like Disney princesses. But a growing body of research suggests that biology may better explain this and other sex-related differences in symptoms. For example, compared with men, women have smaller, more stable airways that are less likely to collapse (and in turn vibrate, making you snore) during sleep. Women also tend to have less fat around their necks, and before menopause they seemingly benefit from the protective effects of estrogen and progesterone, which interact with the respiratory system in a way that aids breathing.

Sources indicate that all things considered, it makes sense why more men than women in the US have this condition, making up about 59% and 41% of obstructive sleep apnea patients, respectively. However, once women go through menopause, which causes their estrogen and progesterone levels to drop, the rate of OSA and the severity of symptoms in this group increases dramatically, Dr. Martin says. Studies have found that anywhere from 47% to 67% of postmenopausal women have obstructive sleep apnea, which is about the same as men in this age range (50 and older). The number of women who actually get diagnosed with the condition is a different story, though—more on that shortly.

According to recent reports, regardless of age, however, women still deal with more sleep apnea–related symptoms than men, Dr. Martin adds, even if they have a less severe form of the condition. This is likely because women have more “subtle breathing disturbances” during sleep that hurt the overall quality of their rest compared with men, Dr. Martin says.

In a recent development, because women often don’t experience “classic” OSA symptoms, they end up being misdiagnosed or dismissed. “When [men] walk into a physician’s office and say they’re sleepy and they snore, they get a diagnostic test right away,” Dr. Martin says. “When a woman walks in and says, ‘I don’t sleep well, and I’m very fatigued during the day,’ they don’t often get referred” for screening. In fact, research suggests that men are nine times more likely to be referred for diagnostic testing than women.

Women with OSA commonly have their symptoms misattributed to conditions like depression, anxiety, insomnia, and menopause or even medication side effects, indicates Dr. Shelgikar, who is also a neurology professor at the University of Michigan Medical School. Not to mention women can have these other conditions as well, which might make their sleep apnea not only harder to detect but also worsen it. Take the double whammy that is insomnia and OSA: Having both of these disorders at the same time is more common among women than men, Dr. Martin says, and in some cases they may be given a sleep aid (such as diphenhydramine or a benzodiazepine) that can further relax their throat muscles, exacerbating their sleep apnea and leaving them even more oxygen-deprived.

Recent findings suggest that and it doesn’t help that, as we talked about earlier, the diagnostic criteria for OSA are largely based on how the condition presents in men. “When we diagnose sleep apnea, we require one of two things to happen: A breathing interruption has to be associated either with a drop in oxygen levels or a brief awakening from sleep,” Dr. Martin claims. “Women don’t have those very deep drops in oxygen levels that men do. So that means that the way we define the disease itself kind of biases us towards diagnosing it more in men than women.” What’s more, Medicare, which the vast majority of Americans ages 65 and older rely on for health insurance, only recognizes a sleep apnea diagnosis if a person has those steep drops in oxygen, Dr. Martin says. Those typical mid-slumber wake-ups don’t count on their own. So even “the criteria that Medicare forces people to use to define sleep apnea is very male-centric,” she adds.

Home sleep apnea tests, which are becoming increasingly common as a cheaper alternative to the gold standard in-lab exams, are also more prone to miss the condition in women. Because women tend to have fewer and milder events than men, these at-home tests may not be able to diagnose sleep apnea as accurately in this population, Dr. Martin claims. They can be even more inaccurate in women with insomnia. These individuals “may not get enough sleep to get an accurate diagnosis,” she says, “so if they wear [the monitor] for six hours, but they’re only sleeping for four of them, it may look like they have less sleep apnea than they really do.”.

According to recent reports, that’s all to say that sleep apnea is likely much more common among women than the available data suggests, experts tell SELF. And that reality reveals a sobering point: A lot of women with this condition probably aren’t receiving the care they need, a delay that can, for some people, snowball into an avalanche of additional yet preventable health issues.

Sources indicate that if left untreated, sleep apnea can have downstream effects on your health, particularly your heart, states Atul Malhotra, MD, research chief of pulmonary, critical care, and sleep medicine at UC San Diego Health. Every time you stop breathing, your body responds to the lack of oxygen by releasing the stress hormone adrenaline to jolt you awake so you take a breath. This happens really quickly; you are typically up for just a few seconds and probably won’t even remember it the next morning.

Over time this constant stress strains your cardiovascular system, Dr. Malhotra says, which may increase your risk for high blood pressure, heart attack, stroke, irregular heartbeat, and heart failure. Although the evidence is mixed, some research suggests that it’s more common for women with severe sleep apnea to experience cardiovascular complications than it is for men. Studies also show that women tend to have more health conditions upon diagnosis than men do, including thyroid disease, asthma, and depression. This raises the classic “chicken or the egg” question, but either way treating OSA can only help.

Because obstructive sleep apnea leads to low-quality shut-eye, it is also associated with memory and cognition concerns and poor daytime alertness, which can boost the likelihood of car and workplace accidents (for certain high-risk jobs like those in the transportation and construction industries), Dr. Shelgikar says. Perhaps less discussed is how untreated sleep apnea affects our ability to care for ourselves and maintain relationships. “We don’t do a good job thinking about sleep apnea as a potential cause of mental health symptoms,” Dr. Martin says. In fact, research indicates that managing OSA could actually help some people dealing with anxiety and depression improve their symptoms.

Industry observers note that as researchers continue searching for answers, Dr. Martin points to a silver lining: There’s good evidence to suggest that women “benefit at least as much as men, if not more” from sleep apnea treatment, which is why it’s important to know what to look out for.

Although you’re quite literally working against decades of medical bias, it’s still possible to receive a sleep apnea diagnosis if you’re equipped with the right intel.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to office pod brand Framery, when companies resize or move, desks and meeting-room furniture often aren’t deemed “worth the cost of moving” and are discarded during the process.

Framery explained that the EU and US discard 11 million tonnes of furniture a year.

Specifically, the brand points to a study for the European Environmental Bureau, which found that in the EU, 80 to 90 per cent of office furniture is burned or landfilled.

According to the Environmental Protection Agency, in the US, less than one per cent is recycled.

Framery aims to tackle this issue with its office pod subscription service, presenting a more environmentally-friendly alternative to disposing of office furniture when a lease runs out, for example.

According to recent reports, “The ‘fast furniture’ trend means 80 per cent of furniture ends up in landfills,” said Framery’s chief design officer, Joonas Vartola. “We wanted to create a pod that’s part of the solution, not the problem.”.

“Framery pods are built for heavy use, keeping them in the field for tens of thousands of sessions and out of landfills,” Vartola added.

For example, if there’s an increase in staff and more pods are needed, or if an office’s layout changes.

The scheme covers the full range of its signature line pods, from one-person phone booths to meeting pods.

According to Saija Serpola, managing director and founding partner at IR Partners, using the pods has enabled increased flexibility and reduced financial risk when investing in additional office furniture.

“We can terminate, increase, or change the solution as our organisation develops.”.

Framery pods are built from mono-materials, including steel, aluminium, glass and PET.

In a recent development, “Our pods with heavy-duty, high-quality materials engineered to withstand wear and tear,” said Vartola. “It’s all about reducing waste, from design to decades of use.”.

As part of the scheme, when a change is required, the pods are dismantled, shipped and rebuilt, rather than discarded into landfill.

Recent findings suggest that according to Framery, each pod is designed for disassembly, with all parts replaceable and recyclable. This includes everything from interior panels, glass, upholstery, carpet, ventilation units and seals.

During refurbishment, each pod is restored to as-new condition and delivered to its next office with a lifetime warranty.

“That is a manufacturing question before it is a commercial one, and it is settled years earlier, on the drawing board.”.

To learn more, visit Framery’s website.

Can Swapping Out Your Plasma Slow the Aging Process?

📅 17 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (908 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, discovering the fountain of youth is an age-old pursuit (pun not intended).
  • But before you start googling “plasma clinics near me,” it’s notable to look past the headlines to what the study’s saying, and what it means—and doesn’t mean—about latest plasma as an anti-aging elixir.
  • Industry observers note that plasma is more than just the liquid that surrounds the red and white blood cells in your bloodstream.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, discovering the fountain of youth is an age-old pursuit (pun not intended). One of the latest clock-reversing experiments causing a buzz is a technique called therapeutic plasma exchange, a procedure that filters and replaces the liquid portion of your blood. A 2025 study in Aging Cell suggests the technique could lower biological age by two and a half years.

But before you start googling “plasma clinics near me,” it’s notable to look past the headlines to what the study’s saying, and what it means—and doesn’t mean—about latest plasma as an anti-aging elixir.

Industry observers note that plasma is more than just the liquid that surrounds the red and white blood cells in your bloodstream. Although it’s mostly water, it’s also rich in proteins, metabolites, hormones, and inflammatory signals—molecules that reflect and influence what’s happening across your organ systems, Andrea Maier, MD, PhD, geriatrician and board member of the Academy for Health and Lifespan Research, tells SELF.

Industry observers note that “It’s a transport system like DHL, a vehicle to bring things from your brain to your muscles, from kidney to lungs, and so on. So it’s fluid with lots of information,” she indicates.

This makes it a smart focal point for longevity studies because it can capture a wide-angle view of your body’s internal state, also sometimes called your “biological age.” By measuring changes in the levels of thousands of circulating proteins in your plasma, you can get some sense of how well you’re functioning.

What that means is you may be 40, but your biology acts more like that of a 30-year-old—or a 50-year-old. It’s not a fixed or precise measurement, but it’s helpful health information, Keenan Walker, PhD, senior investigator at the National Institute on Aging, tells SELF.

“There’s no one biological age, but people try to estimate it,” he says. “And what studies have found is that people whose biological age is older than their chronological age are at greater risk for chronic conditions, diseases, and mortality.”.

About 15 years ago, researchers started exploring the connection between plasma and the aging process. This led to experiments using a process called parabiosis, a surgical technique that links together the circulatory systems of two different organisms. In studies, researchers would stitch together the systems of old mice and young mice, with the hypothesis that if you circulated younger plasma in an older organism, the older organism’s body would reap the benefits.

And the studies did show that. Older mice who received the plasma of younger mice had more resilience to tissue and organ stress. This led to the development of using plasma exchange as a way to treat certain autoimmune diseases, neurological disorders, and blood cancers.

Recent findings suggest that “So everything really came out of that question: Is there something in our circulation we could get rid of or infuse into it to be able to live longer?” indicates Dr. Maier. But there’s not a definitive answer to that question—yet.

In a recent development, in the Aging Cell study, researchers enrolled 42 people and exchanged their plasma with purified albumin (a blood protein) and saline. Some participants also got a type of immune therapy called IVIG added in. Researchers measured changes in their bodies with advanced lab tests that track aging at the molecular level.

At first glance, the results look significant: Some people in the study reduced their biological age by roughly 2.5 years. But Dr. Maier points out that this data comes from the middle of the study, not the end.

“If you are digging a little bit deeper, this ‘2.5 years younger’ is comparing people at midterm to the baseline, not at the end of the study and the baseline. At the end, the effect was nearly gone,” she notes.

Part of the reason for this, indicates Dr. Maier, is you overwhelm your body when you take all its plasma out and reintroduce different plasma. The influx of young cells can produce a shift in your biological age, but then your body starts experiencing stress as it adapts to this major change, and your biomarkers swing back to what they were before. In other words, you may get some rejuvenation in the short-term, but it’s temporary.

Another noteworthy detail about the study was the health of the participants, notes Dr. Walker. “Those who were less healthy saw a stronger intervention effect,” he says. “So I think it'll be crucial to find out for whom this works.”.

As a concept, both Drs. Maier and Walker see some promise in blood-based interventions for improving overall health but hope to see a more personalized approach rather than a generalized non-specific plasma filtering process.

“I would call this a phase 1 study,” says Dr. Maier. “We’ve basically learned that we can safely do it, and now we have to see it in much bigger studies and look at the long-term effect. It’s not a crazy idea. It’s absolutely grounded in lots of evidence, but not for everybody. It needs to be more precise. The future is great in our field, and this is the first tiny step, but we should absolutely not implement it now in clinical practice because it is so rough on the body. I love innovation, and I love this study, but I think the future will give something else.”.

The conversion of a Victorian hospital into facilities for the University of Edinburgh, shortlisted for the RIAS Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award, features in this video by photographer Jim Stephenson.

The film forms part of a series being published by Dezeen in collaboration with the Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland (RIAS) to highlight the annual award’s 2026 shortlist.

In the video, viewers are introduced to the Edinburgh Futures Institute by London-based Bennetts Associates, which involved the revitalisation of the Category A-listed building to create teaching spaces for the university, including a 450-seat auditorium.

Central to the building’s new function was the opening up of the programme to the public, highlighted by the creation of a public square at its front.

“A large part of the project was, of course, rescuing the building,” studio founder Rab Bennetts said.

“Our mission, if you like, was to come back and reopen that main entrance, give it a sense of purpose again, open up the space to the street and make it a public space.”.

Established in 2002, the Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award is an annual award that highlights Scottish projects, with this year’s winner set to be announced on 26 November.

Industry observers note that comprising three reuse projects, RIAS remarked this year’s shortlisted projects tap into “key conversations around community, collaboration, retrofit and reuse”. Shortlisted alongside the Edinburgh Futures Institute is the Paisley Central Library by Collective Architecture and the Tarlair Outdoor Pool Pavilion by Studio Octopi.

Last year’s winner was a public park renewed by studios Stallan-Brand and LDA Design.

Film and photography by Jim Stephenson.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Architecture studio BIG has unveiled a hotel building with a stepped, zigzagging design that will function as a “gateway” to the Siegenthalergut urban district in Thun, Switzerland.

Together with landscape architect August + Margrith Künzel, MASSIVE designed the 13,000-square-metre Nachwachsende Stadt (Growing City) development, which will form a key section of the new district.

Nachwachsende Stadt will be comprised of four timber buildings, which will house two hotels, residences and commercial spaces. It will be located on a prominent site in Thun’s new Siegenthalergut district, close to the future Swiss Football Association headquarters.

The most striking of the four buildings is a timber block with a cantilevered corner volume that will be home to both a three-star and four-star hotel.

The stepped design creates terraces that are mirrored by the upside-down design of the cantilevered volume, forming a central rift that will be glazed to let light into the building,.

“The Siegenthalergut site is an opportunity to create more than just a new development,” BIG partner Sören Grünert noted.

“It allows Thun to grow without losing its character while also raising its profile on the national stage,” he continued.

“With the future home of the Swiss Football Association right next door, the neighbourhood will become the city’s calling card: a community, a gateway, and a landmark all at once.”.

According to recent reports, the hotel building will have commercial spaces along the street and a rooftop restaurant. It will be complemented by three residential buildings, which will also be built from timber but have a more traditional gridded design.

Here, projecting bays and set-back terraces will help to create privacy for the residents, whose homes will overlook a shared courtyard.

MASSIVE used timber to help reduce the buildings’ carbon footprint, designing the development for “future disassembly and reuse” so that it can be adapted over time.

The development will also have green roofs, photovoltaic panels and rainwater retention systems to help it achieve a targeted SNBS Gold standard.

Construction on the Nachwachsende Stadt is expected to start in 2028.

SIGNIFICANT also recently designed a “modular blueprint” for Refugee City in Rwanda and the cloud-like Tirana Fountain Plaza above a public park.

#80031. Spring Allergies Can Cause Headaches. Here’s How to Deal

Spring Allergies Can Cause Headaches. Here’s How to Deal

📅 17 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1084 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A stuffy nose and itchy, watery eyes are spring-allergy cornerstones—but they’re not the only symptoms that herald a pollen influx for some people.
  • In fact, the same immune response that fills your nose with snot or leaves you sneezing up a storm can make your head throb.
  • According to recent reports, if you have spring allergies and breathe in pollen, “your immune system perceives it as a foreign invader,” Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A stuffy nose and itchy, watery eyes are spring-allergy cornerstones—but they’re not the only symptoms that herald a pollen influx for some people. You might not immediately suspect a pulsing headache is due to allergies, but experts say it’s a common occurrence.

In fact, the same immune response that fills your nose with snot or leaves you sneezing up a storm can make your head throb. That’s especially true “if you have multiple seasonal allergies, for instance to grass and tree pollen; live near farms; or spend a lot of time outside during allergy season, being bombarded by pollen,” Beth Oller, MD, a family medicine physician in Stockton, Kansas, tells SELF. Keep reading to learn why allergies can spark headaches, plus how to tell if your head pain is allergy-related and find relief.

According to recent reports, if you have spring allergies and breathe in pollen, “your immune system perceives it as a foreign invader,” Dr. Oller says, and releases a bunch of inflammatory chemicals like histamine. The resulting inflammation triggers swelling in your nasal cavities, which are connected to your sinuses, Rekha Raveendran, MD, allergist and immunologist at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, tells SELF. The sinuses extend behind the cheekbones, eyes, and bridge of the nose, and up into the forehead—so when they get puffy, you can wind up with a sensation of facial pressure and also headache, she explains.

At the same time, experiencing the effects of spring allergies may spark migraine attacks in those with migraine. The surge of inflammation and congestion can irritate a nearby nerve that plays a role in migraine, and allergy-driven fatigue and insomnia can be migraine triggers in and of themselves. Research suggests that among people with migraine, those who also have allergies tend to have worse, more frequent attacks than those who don’t.

Recent findings suggest that an allergy headache typically feels like a dull throbbing in your temples, cheeks, or forehead, and makes your face feel heavy. It comes along with congestion, Dr. Oller says, and lying down or tilting your head can increase the pressure. (FYI: This is the same kind of pain as you’d get with a sinus headache, which is caused by a viral or bacterial infection in your sinuses—both lead to mucus buildup and swelling within the sinuses.).

Industry observers note that by contrast, migraine attacks (whether or not they’re precipitated by allergies) trigger intense pain on one side of the head. They often come along with nausea, and sensitivity to light and sound, which you would not typically find with allergy headaches, Dr. Raveendran indicates. Meanwhile, tension headaches tend to feel more like a band squeezing around the head, and cluster headaches spark a surge of pain in or around one eye.

It has been revealed that if you get walloped with allergy headaches each year, Dr. Oller suggests starting on an oral antihistamine medication right about now. Pollen counts are rising, and antihistamines take a week or two of daily use to kick in, she explains. The non-drowsy options work best for daytime—think: cetirizine (Zyrtec), levocetirizine (Xyzal), loratadine (Claritin), or fexofenadine (Allegra). You can use the sleepiness-inducing diphenhydramine (Benadryl) at night, but just know that you shouldn’t make a habit of relying on it as a sleep aid.

It has been revealed that both doctors suggest pairing oral allergy meds with a nasal corticosteroid spray like fluticasone (Flonase) or triamcinolone (Nasocort). “They hit those mucus membranes and help decrease inflammation in that region,” Dr. Oller says. It’s best to take both drugs daily throughout allergy season, she adds, not just when you think you need them. (If your headaches are barely alleviated, or the pollen counts in your area are sky-high, you may also be able to safely increase your dose of these allergy meds to boost their efficacy.).

The less pollen that enters your airspace, the fewer symptoms you’ll experience. But you don’t have to stay cooped up to cut your exposure. Keeping your windows closed, using a high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filter in your HVAC system (or a portable air purifier that has one), and vacuuming often can make a difference, according to Dr. Oller.

According to recent reports, whenever you do spend ample time outside, Dr. Oller notes to rinse off once you get home. This way, you’re not inhaling pollen any longer than you have to. While you’re at it, “shower your sinuses too,” Dr. Oller adds, with a nasal saline spray or Neti Pot. This helps clear some mucus to release pressure and offer temporary relief, Dr. Raveendran says.

If the congestion is making it feel like your face is chock-full of mucus, you might be tempted to reach for an OTC oral decongestant. But take note: While pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) can be helpful, it’s not recommended to use it more than a few days in a row, and isn’t a good choice if you have high blood pressure, Dr. Raveendran says. It’s a stimulant that can make some people feel jittery, or cause a fast heart rate or insomnia.

Nasal decongestants, which include phenylephrine- or oxymetazoline-based sprays (like Afrin and Vicks Sinex), can open up your nose fast but should only be used for three days at a time max, Dr. Raveendran adds. “There’s a risk of rebound congestion that leads to overall worsening of symptoms and addiction to the nasal decongestants,” she indicates.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes you just need in-the-moment relief for the head pain. In that case, you can pop an OTC pain reliever like ibuprofen (Advil), naproxen (Aleve), or acetaminophen (Tylenol), Dr. Oller states. The former two may be better at resolving allergy headaches because they combat inflammation. But it’s not advised to take these non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for more than 10 days straight (unless your doctor tells you otherwise) because of potential effects on your stomach and kidneys. Tylenol, by contrast, is generally safer to take long-term, though shouldn’t be combined with alcohol due to the risk for liver damage.

Sources indicate that if you find that your allergy headaches have you reaching for pain relievers more than a few days in a row, check in with your primary care doctor or allergist. They may recommend a more intensive treatment, like prescription steroids, or suggest seeing an ear, nose, and throat doctor or neurologist, in case something else might be behind your head pain.

#80027. Tech Report: Can You Actually ‘Boost’ Your Metabolism?

📅 17 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1442 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Can You Actually ‘Boost’ Your Metabolism?

📅 17 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1442 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that few bodily processes are as focused on and as misunderstood as metabolism.
  • Recent findings suggest that the truth?
  • Metabolism is commonly thought of as the mechanism that controls your weight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that few bodily processes are as focused on and as misunderstood as metabolism. It seems like just about everyone wants to “boost” or “speed up” their metabolism in the hopes of burning more calories and, as a result, losing body fat. In reality, this is not an easy task, but you wouldn’t know that from the countless TikToks claiming it’s as simple as taking a shot of apple cider vinegar, hopping into an infrared sauna, or braving a cold plunge.

Recent findings suggest that the truth? Many of these supposed hacks don’t have much research backing them up, and the ones that do won’t meaningfully move the needle when it comes to your weight. Improving your metabolism actually boils down to a few basic tenets that aren’t flashy or sexy but can have long-term benefits for your overall health and well-being. We’ll get into all that, but first, a little background on what your metabolism even is.

Metabolism is commonly thought of as the mechanism that controls your weight. Having a “fast” metabolism means your body burns calories rapidly, making it easier to maintain or lose weight, while having a “slow” metabolism means you gain pounds more easily and have a harder time taking them off. This isn’t wrong, per se, but it doesn’t tell the whole story. Your metabolism is the way your body turns food into energy. This energy is then used to power your heart and lungs, build and repair tissue, regulate hormones, and perform other critical functions.

Put more succinctly, “metabolism is all the chemical processes that keep our body alive and functioning,” explains Jonathan Gabison, MD, an assistant professor of family medicine at the University of Michigan who is board-certified in obesity medicine.

For example, about 20% of the energy your metabolism provides goes to your brain, building neurotransmitters and keeping signals going, so having an efficient metabolism is critical for cognitive health.

Recent findings suggest that in short, yes. Your metabolism is influenced by loads of factors, from genetics and age to weight. But that doesn’t mean your metabolism is fixed. It’s actually highly modifiable, says Shebani Sethi, MD, a clinical associate professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford University and the founding director of the world’s first academic metabolic psychiatry clinical program.

Sources indicate that that mentioned, taking shots of apple cider vinegar in the morning or picking up “metabolism-boosting” supplements won’t do the trick. Research reveals that improving your metabolism requires consistent long-term habits. Here are five that can make an impact.

Industry observers note that every time you move your body, it burns calories and raises your metabolism—both during the moment and for a period afterward. Think of your metabolism like a pie: Two thirds of the energy you use every day is devoted to keeping you alive (that’s your basal metabolic rate), and the rest goes toward digesting food and moving your body. Being more active is the most straightforward way to up your metabolism. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate intensity physical activity a week.

This can include dedicated exercise, like a jog, hike, or workout class. (The CDC recommends that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate intensity physical activity a week.) But it also extends to all the movement you do outside of formal exercise, known as NEAT (non-exercise activity thermogenesis). Increasing your daily step count, prioritizing physical hobbies like gardening and walking your dog, or even taking on more household chores and grocery runs all count toward upping your overall movement.

According to recent reports, strength training helps build and maintain muscle mass. Muscle tissue is metabolically active, which means sustaining it burns more calories than maintaining fat tissue. Therefore, having more muscle mass will give your metabolism a slight boost.

Sources indicate that by strength training you’re also improving your overall health. For instance, since muscle tissue uses the majority of the glucose in your bloodstream, more muscle mass can increase your body’s capacity to use glucose and help prevent blood sugar spikes. Plus, research has shown that having more muscle helps improve insulin sensitivity, including in individuals without diabetes.

Those same CDC exercise guidelines suggest including at least two days of strength training every week. That can include body-weight moves like push-ups and lunges; lifting weights with dumbbells, kettlebells, barbells, or cable machines; or utilizing resistance bands. Dr. Gabison states what’s most important is being consistent with your exercise routine, so it’s best to choose workouts you’re likely to stick with. And remember, if you’re just starting out, it’s important not to push yourself too hard early on and risk injury.

Industry observers note that protein is having a major moment right now. While things may be getting a little out of hand (hello, protein popcorn), consuming sufficient amounts of high-quality protein has well-established benefits for your metabolism. That’s because the nutrient is the building block of muscle, so eating enough of it helps support muscle growth and maintenance, especially if you’re resistance training.

Sources indicate that protein also has the highest thermic effect of all three macronutrients, meaning digesting it burns more calories than carbohydrates or fats. Plus, it’s the most satiating macro, so increasing your protein intake can help you feel fuller and fend off cravings, which may help with weight management.

However, balance is key. Sun Kim, MD, MS, a board-certified endocrinologist and associate professor of medicine at Stanford, says doctors and health care providers have different viewpoints on how much protein is enough for optimal health. In her opinion, “most Americans eat plenty of protein without trying,” she says, cautioning that consuming excessive amounts won’t magically speed up your metabolism and could even worsen insulin sensitivity in some cases. So unless you’re extremely active, there’s no need to get hundreds of grams a day.

For most healthy adults, the recommended dietary allowance for protein is 0.8 grams per kilogram of body weight per day. That means a 120-pound person needs roughly 43 grams of protein a day, which is about what you’d find in two four-ounce hamburger patties. If you incorporate some protein into every snack and meal throughout the day, you should easily hit the mark. That noted, some groups need more. People who are pregnant, breastfeeding, or highly active may need up to 2 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day. Older adults and those taking GLP-1s should also be mindful of their intake, as reduced appetite can lead to inadequate protein intake and muscle loss, particularly when coupled with reduced physical activity.

An often-overlooked habit for better metabolism is getting quality sleep. A lack of sleep dysregulates your metabolism, causing a cascade of concerns, including worsened glucose management, more intense hunger the next day, and reduced energy expenditure. (Sleepy people are less likely to move their bodies.) When this happens consistently, it can lead to an increased risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease. Sleep also has an impact on hormones that can slow down the metabolism.

There isn’t a specific number of hours you should sleep each night, but research shows that most adults do best with seven to nine hours of quality rest most evenings.

Recent findings suggest that prolonged stress keeps your cortisol (stress hormone) levels chronically elevated, which can break down muscle tissue and slow your metabolism. Constantly pulling out your hair can also disrupt your appetite-regulating hormones, triggering cravings that may prompt you to eat more. All of these things can affect your weight. Research shows chronic stress can increase your risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, and related cardiometabolic complications too.

Recent findings suggest that there is, sadly, no quick fix for reducing stress, so some trial and error might be required to figure out what works best for you. Some places to start are doing yoga, meditating, practicing breathing exercises, going for walks outside, journaling, spending time with loved ones, engaging in relaxing hobbies, or starting therapy to talk through whatever is weighing on you.

Sure, supporting a healthy metabolism can increase the number of calories you burn and help with weight management. But it can also improve what’s known as your metabolic health, which encompasses measures such as blood pressure, cholesterol, insulin sensitivity, and total body fat. Having good metabolic health is essential for preventing chronic diseases such as type 2 diabetes and heart disease. The healthier your metabolism, the more calories you burn and the better your metabolic health.

#80025. "All over the world, buildings designed to be explored in 3D are subject to restrictions"

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1283 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dezeen ↗ Open Full Page

"All over the world, buildings designed to be explored in 3D are subject to restrictions"

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1283 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Controversy over visitors having to pay to access the walkable roof at the upcoming Shanghai Grand Opera House brings into focus the need for architects to be realistic about how buildings operate, writes Aaron Betksy.
  • Sources indicate that the beauty of many recent Chinese buildings is that they are also landscapes.
  • Ma Yansong’s buildings are often hills that you are invited to climb: the new Shenzhen Bay Cultural Center is a case in point, as is the Quzhou Sports Center, which actually is five different scalable hills, but his oldest major building, the Harbin Opera House of 2015, also offers a path over the auditorium.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Controversy over visitors having to pay to access the walkable roof at the upcoming Shanghai Grand Opera House brings into focus the need for architects to be realistic about how buildings operate, writes Aaron Betksy.

Sources indicate that the beauty of many recent Chinese buildings is that they are also landscapes. You can walk up to them, around them, and through them, but also over them.

Ma Yansong’s buildings are often hills that you are invited to climb: the new Shenzhen Bay Cultural Center is a case in point, as is the Quzhou Sports Center, which actually is five different scalable hills, but his oldest major building, the Harbin Opera House of 2015, also offers a path over the auditorium. The Kowloon High Speed Train Station, designed by Andrew Bromberg of Aedas, is meant to be a continuous curve rising over the waiting hall you can ascend to view over to Hong Kong Island.

And now Snøhetta’s just-completed Shanghai Opera House offers you a cantilevered stair with a view back over the river to the city.

Many building owners who have paid a little extra to get that architectural rizz have realized, once they see their building overwhelmed by selfie takers, that they can monetize their outlooks.

There’s only one problem: sooner or later, you will hit a barrier, usually makeshift and consisting of moveable fences and lots of yellow and black tape.

According to recent reports, sometimes the restrictions are monetary. Many building owners who have paid a little extra to get that architectural rizz have realized, once they see their building overwhelmed by selfie takers, that they can monetize their outlooks and prospects. The Shanghai Opera House is the latest case: to ascend that-stairway-almost-to-heaven you must pay 50 RMB, or about eight bucks.

Recent findings suggest that that last move has raised the consciousness of the masses to a much higher degree than the inability to climb Mount Ma in various cities. The digisphere is not happy. Apparently, people feel that photographing themselves against an urban view should be a right, even if the institution giving them that opportunity invested (albeit, in this case, mainly through state funds) in making that experience possible.

Nor is this a problem only in China: all over the world, buildings that were designed to be explored in three dimensions are often subject to restrictions. The fluidity of which architects dream drowns in a sea of concerns about safety and security.

In Europe, the restrictions are a bit more akin to the maze airports have put in your way between security and the gates: you can get to the top of MVRDV’s Depot in Rotterdam or Herzog & de Meuron’s Elbphilharmonie in Hamburg for free, but you have to figure out how, and are meant to be tempted to buy at least a drink along the way.

In our experience economy, that seems par for the parcours to me. Space and views are among the most valuable luxuries on offer, so, until the revolution comes, I do not see the major deal.

A both bigger and smaller concern is the barriers themselves. Even those who confront them in Shanghai and don’t mind forking over the yuan find that the kluges stand in the way not only of free access, but also of the views and of the architecture.

You can ignore the Eyes in the Sky hidden in the ceiling, but not the fences.

According to recent reports, that is because the architects never intended the fences to be there in the first place, so they did not design them into the building. They are the most obtrusive part of the many signs, furnishings, and security devices that festoon buildings especially in China, but all over the world as well.

According to recent reports, the architect Theo Deutinger has written a wonderful compendium, Handbook of Tyranny, listing and diagraming many of the devices that control our movements. Many of them we do not notice, but those that are added after construction stick out the most. You can ignore the Eyes in the Sky hidden in the ceiling, but not the fences.

Ironically, part of the reason they are so obvious in China and other Asian countries is because until recently there were so many fewer of them. When the Harbin Opera House opened a little over a decade ago you could clamber all over it, and the same was true of the Kowloon train station.

Industry observers note that in recent years, local authorities have become concerned about the same problems that have restricted flows in the Western world. That is largely because of heightened accountability: you can’t easily sue if you trip in China, but local authorities can face consequences from government over mishaps in buildings they oversee – and architects there tell me this is increasingly common.

To be clear, beyond the aesthetic concerns these developments are not entirely negative. Accessibility provisions have often been poor in China, but recently ramps and other devices are opening more spaces to those with mobility issues – including toddlers and older people who might enjoy these urban landscapes the most. Architects design tiered complexity at the risk of eliminating many customers, as Steven Holl, for instance, found out in the case of his Brooklyn Library.

The solution should be relatively simple: architects should design both accessibility and risk-avoidance into their vertical landscapes. Ma’s Lucas Museum in Los Angeles and its surrounding park, designed by Mia Lehrer, already do so (pictured left). There is no reason beyond economics and design complexity that people should not be guided and seduced up and over buildings, even if they might have to pay for that privilege.

When Zaha Hadid started on her folds and later curves, she dreamed of a truly open architecture in which urban life would move without barriers.

That leaves only a deeper matter, which is that of the difficulty of fulfilling the promise of fluid space. When Zaha Hadid started on her folds and later curves, she dreamed of a truly open architecture in which urban life would move without barriers in and out of covered and even conditioned places. Blobitecture or parametricism offered the same prospects, and Wolf Prix has been screaming for an “open architecture of the open eye, the open mind, the open heart” for decades.

Objective reality stands in the way. Buildings are still buildings – both because of the limits of what structures and conditioning systems can do, leading to the hoary problem of where you put a door, or even a toilet, with sufficient headroom in a blob – and because somebody pays for them.

Inside, as Rem Koolhaas once mentioned, “all conditioned space is conditional” and outside we are finding that the same is true. You have to pay to play, or for right of way.

As is so often the case, the mountable building landscapes that have been constructed with increasing frequency and at larger and larger scales in the last few decades are more promissory notes for a future open society than built utopias. You can go with the flow and climb any building or mountain, but sooner or later economic and regulatory reality will bring you back down to earth.

Sources indicate that aaron Betsky is a senior design associate at Carlo Ratti Associati, a visiting professor at Kean University and a visiting lecturer at the University of Pennsylvania. He was previously a professor at Virginia Tech School of Architecture and Design and president of the School of Architecture at Taliesin. He has written more than a dozen books on architecture, design and art, including Landscrapers: Building with the Land, published in 2002.
