13 Black Women Share How They Found the Strength to Survive—and Thrive—With Breast Cancer

📅 18 Oct 2021 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4401 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When it comes to Black women’s breast health, the statistics rarely tell a hopeful story.
  • Industry observers note that but here’s what the numbers will never capture: the phone calls at 3 a.m., the head-shaving parties, the therapy sessions that cracked something open, the moment a woman looks at her daughter or granddaughter and decides they are reason enough to fight.
  • Sources indicate that the stories below belong to 13 Black women who refused to be reduced to a statistic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When it comes to Black women’s breast health, the statistics rarely tell a hopeful story. Black women are diagnosed with breast cancer at a younger median age (60, compared with 62 for white women) and are 38% more likely to die from the disease. They have the lowest survival rate for every known stage of breast cancer. And about one in five Black women with breast cancer are diagnosed with hard-to-treat triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), more than any other racial or ethnic group.

Industry observers note that but here’s what the numbers will never capture: the phone calls at 3 a.m., the head-shaving parties, the therapy sessions that cracked something open, the moment a woman looks at her daughter or granddaughter and decides they are reason enough to fight. Black women have always been more than a data point, and perhaps nowhere is that truer than in the way they face, survive, and remake their lives after a breast cancer diagnosis.

Sources indicate that the stories below belong to 13 Black women who refused to be reduced to a statistic. They are individuals with careers, children, humor, faith, rage, and joy whose experiences with breast cancer changed them in ways both devastating and profound. In finding their own paths through treatment and beyond, they’ve built something the data can’t quantify: community, purpose, and a hard-won blueprint for survival they’re passing on to every woman who comes after them.

In a recent development, monique Bass, 53, had always been proactive about her health. A single mother of twin sons and grandmother of four, she started getting annual mammograms at 40. But it was a self-exam at 47 while lying in bed one night that changed everything. She found a lump that didn’t feel right.

Industry observers note that what followed were three tissue biopsies of the lump over three years, each coming back benign. Doctors wanted to keep monitoring. Bass pushed back. The lump was growing, and she knew her body well enough to realize something was wrong. She insisted they remove the lump (a procedure called a lumpectomy) and test it. The diagnosis: stage 1 invasive ductal carcinoma that was aggressive enough to require immediate chemotherapy.

Bass got the call while sitting in a car wash. “I felt like I was in The Twilight Zone,” she claims. “Not in a million years did I think I would ever hear the words, ‘You have cancer.’” The timing made everything harder. It was 2020, the height of the pandemic, so she navigated much of her journey alone. Adding “another emotional layer,” she was also going through a divorce. Treatment included four rounds of doxorubicin, four rounds of paclitaxel, and 21 radiation treatments. Losing her hair hit the hardest. “But the silver lining is that it grew back even more beautifully after treatment,” Bass says.

In a recent development, throughout it all her faith anchored her. “I’m not a deeply religious person, but I believe in God, and I knew he had me in the palm of his hand,” Bass says. On the other side of treatment, she founded What’s Behind the Bra?, a New Jersey nonprofit that distributes comfort care packages to breast cancer patients year-round and hosts a weekly podcast of the same name every Sunday at 7:30 p.m. ET.

Jaqueline Beale, 64, comes from a family with a long history of cancer, including her mother, who had breast cancer. That’s why it wasn’t a huge surprise when, at 40, she found a lump during a breast self-exam. Even though a sonogram and mammogram came back clear, it was obvious that something wasn’t right, so Beale got a biopsy.

When the radiologist called with her result—stage 1 breast cancer, which means the cancer hadn’t spread beyond where the abnormal cells had developed—she could hear a lot of noise in the background. He noted, “I’m in Fresh York trying to hail a cab, but you have breast cancer. You need to find a breast surgeon.” Despite the bluntness, Beale says she couldn’t help but find the humor in the situation, which is something she carried with her through treatment.

“I made sure that I surrounded myself with laughter and love,” she says, “and I told my family that I knew they loved me, but I also needed a lot of laughter to get through it.”.

Sources indicate that she recalls one incident in an elevator after her sister had taken her to a chemo treatment. “I had been sick as a dog after, and a woman got in and asked if I was okay. My sister said, ‘Oh, she’s fine. She’s just got a little bit of cancer.’ The woman looked horrified, but I laughed. My family knew that their sense of humor is what I needed.”.

In a recent development, annita White, 51, was five months late for her mammogram. As a single mother of two boys, a higher education administrator, and a first-year PhD student, she always had something more pressing. When she finally went, she expected the usual letter in the mail saying everything was fine. Instead, she got a call. There was a mass that hadn’t been there before.

According to recent reports, by the time the biopsy came back, she already knew. A technician had commented on how hard the mass was, and White felt the diagnosis in her spirit before the words were ever spoken. The confirmation came the next day. “When I got the call, I fell to the floor and cried tears of desperation,” she says. “My first thought was, ‘Lord, I can’t do this.’”.

What followed was hard in every way: chemotherapy, losing her breasts, losing her hair, which had always been full. “Being bald left me feeling vulnerable and insecure,” White says. “Physically, losing my breasts and going through chemotherapy made me feel like my body was no longer my own.” Through it all the fear that drove her was running out of time—time to see her sons become men and to meet her grandchildren someday.

In a recent development, her faith, which she’d been privately wrestling with for years, met her exactly where she was. She’d been asking God to truly show up in her life. “He did,” she indicates. “In the middle of one of the hardest seasons of my life, he carried me through.”.

Three years later White is cancer-free, her hair is back, and she recently finished her PhD. She now walks in her purpose as Dr. Nita, a member of the African American Breast Cancer Alliance survivor network, sharing her story and those of others facing the disease. “What once felt like the end became the beginning of something greater,” she notes.

Marylande Regis, 38, had been in her fresh Georgia home for four months when everything changed. A registered nurse, realtor, wife, and mother of three, she had just stopped breastfeeding her nine-month-old when she found the lump. Her baby had never latched well on that side. When she messaged her provider, the on-call response was that it was probably a clogged milk duct and that she was too young to worry about it being something more serious. Regis didn’t accept that. She called back and left a message, insisting that something was wrong. “Another ob-gyn saw the message and encouraged me to make an office appointment immediately,” she notes. Within two weeks she had a diagnosis: aggressive stage 2B, BRCA1-positive breast cancer. Within two more weeks what had been one tumor and one impacted lymph node had become three tumors and four impacted lymph nodes. Regis was 36.

“I was relieved that I advocated for myself,” she claims. “I was proud that fear didn’t factor into my decision.”.

Industry observers note that what followed was relentless. Regis went through six months of chemotherapy, a bilateral mastectomy, six weeks of radiation, a total hysterectomy (to eliminate her body’s main source of estrogen), and breast reconstruction, all over a span of roughly 18 months. She lost friends to cancer along the way, as well as a cousin diagnosed around the same time. Her faith was, as Regis describes it, “shaken and stirred and flipped every way possible.” She wrote the vital letters. She wrote her own obituary. She was practical about it. “I wanted to be positive, but I am also very realistic,” Regis says.

In a recent development, the hardest part wasn’t any single treatment—it was losing control. As her family’s go-to planner for everything from doctor’s appointments to vacations, she found it foreign to ask for help. But when she told her parents, her mother showed up and never left. “We joke, but my mom never went home,” Regis notes. “This is her house now.” Her husband, Kory, came to every appointment and held steady even through both of them losing their jobs. “He deserves a trophy,” she says.

As the daughter of Haitian immigrants, raised to be everything her parents couldn’t be, Regis claims the fight was never just medical. Today strength looks different than it did before cancer. It looks like making it to the bus stop with her son, who has autism. It looks like seeing her oldest finish nursing school and work toward becoming an ob-gyn. It looks like watching her youngest hit milestones like learning to talk. “I would have missed that if I didn’t fight,” she says. “The clouds are moving. The sun has decided to show itself. I can’t wait to soak it all in.”.

Illness had always been an afterthought for 75-year-old Judy Fambrough-Billingsley. Why would it cross her mind? She walked three miles every day, swam laps all summer, took Zumba classes, and played soccer for 30 years. Judy Fambrough-Billingsley had never smoked or drank, and she didn’t even need to take medication. Being healthy wasn’t something she worked at; it was just who she was. A naturalized American citizen born in Germany, she traveled back to her home country regularly to visit family. Her life was full and active.

Sources indicate that so when she felt a lump—and then another six months later—she ignored them. After all, she’d had a clean mammogram earlier that year. But when she noticed them growing and multiplying, she went back to her doctor. The results were not what she expected.

Industry observers note that “I was shocked,” Fambrough-Billingsley says. She suddenly found herself navigating an entirely latest set of experiences: prescription bottles, hospital procedures, lab processes—the whole medical system. “Being a part of a world where sickness exists had never been my world until now,” she says.

According to recent reports, what carried her through was far older than her diagnosis. She grew up during the Civil Rights Era, the daughter of a successful Black entrepreneur who built his business during tumultuous years in US history. Both her parents were lifetime members of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP). She was president of the NAACP Youth Council and an active member of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. Fambrough-Billingsley knows something about fighting for your life in systems that weren’t built for you.

In a recent development, “Growing up during the Civil Rights Era contributed to this era of fighting,” she indicates. “Never giving up.” That same spirit—the one her parents modeled, the one she fell into during her work as a community organizer and across decades of a life fully lived—is the one she’s bringing to this too. She may still be on her breast cancer journey, but this is not her first fight.

Industry observers note that taylor Johnson was nearly 30 when she found the lump on her left breast. A mom and content creator who loves trying new things and staying active, she went to her primary care doctor, who referred her for an ultrasound and a mammogram. Johnson was denied a mammogram—she was told she was too young. She pushed anyway, got a biopsy (in lieu of the mammogram), and days later, had a diagnosis: stage 2 triple-negative breast cancer.

According to recent reports, “My reaction was a very deep pause, trying to process what my doctor had told me,” Johnson notes. “It then hit me, and all I could do was cry.”.

She’s in the middle of her treatment proposal, which includes six months of chemotherapy, followed by surgery and three weeks of radiation. After finishing chemo Johnson felt confident that would be the hardest part of her journey, both physically and emotionally. But her own health wasn’t her only concern: She knew her five-year-old was watching her every move, and she wanted to stay stable for her daughter. “I was so used to always being the strong one,” Johnson claims. “This definitely tested that.” She held it together not because it came easily, but because she understood what her daughter was absorbing.

According to recent reports, she is grateful for the community that rallied around her while she waited. Weekly prayer calls, rotating visits from family and friends, and a medical team at Mayo Clinic in Arizona that went above and beyond carried her through.

Though Johnson hasn’t finished treatment yet, completing chemo clarified something for her. “It has reassured me how strong I truly am,” she states. Strength, she’s learned, isn’t just physical. The emotional and mental muscle it takes to keep going counts just as much.

Jessica Ncube, 41, built her life around caring for others. A licensed clinical social worker, the co-owner of a mental health practice, and a mom, she was always in motion. Her life revolved around showing up for others and helping them navigate their hardest moments. “Looking back I do not know that I was always receiving,” she states.

In a recent development, her diagnosis came quietly. A routine mammogram caught it; nothing in her body had felt amiss. That silence, Ncube says, is exactly why early detection matters. When she got the news she went into survival mode. “You hear the words, but it takes time for them to land,” she says.

Ncube’s journey started with a lumpectomy. When her margins came back unclear, meaning the pathologist could not determine whether all the cancerous cells were removed, she made the decision to move forward with a double mastectomy with reconstructive surgery. “Losing a part of your body, even when it is lifesaving, is still a loss,” she states. “The hardest part was learning how to sit in both gratitude and grief at the same time.”.

Industry observers note that as someone professionally wired to be strong for others, letting that tendency go was its own kind of work. “Strength became less about holding everything in and more about being honest about what I needed,” Ncube says. Her faith grounded her, and her community revealed up, but she also had to unlearn something deeply familiar. “As a Black woman there is a resilience that is almost ingrained in us,” she says. “I had to learn how to balance that resilience with softness.”.

Industry observers note that after completing treatment Ncube has become more present and deliberate. Her definition of strength has changed entirely. “Strength today is softness. It is honesty. It is allowing myself to receive, to rest, and to not have all the answers,” she claims.

Ameiko Newman, 40, didn’t learn of her diagnosis through a routine screening. She was rushed to the hospital for abdominal pain, and that’s when she learned she had breast cancer. Life before her diagnosis had been stressful, uncertain, a season of not quite knowing where she was headed. In a strange way, cancer gave her direction.

“For me, cancer saved me,” she notes. “It made me a better person. It made me fight harder, push through the hard times and know what I want in life.”.

It has been revealed that newman is still in treatment, receiving chemotherapy and immunotherapy every week, and she is honest about what that looks like: There are good days and bad days. She goes to church faithfully, prays every day, and tries to stay positive through it all.

What has surprised her most is that in the middle of fighting for her own life, she found her purpose: helping others fight for theirs. Newman rebranded her business entirely around that mission and started designing scarves with chemo patients in mind. “I started making them mainly for my Black women because you know we love having style,” she states. But a wide variety of women from all over have since bought them.

She wakes up every day, gets her kids ready, works out, and moves through life. Faith, she says, is what makes that possible. Her message to any Black woman who’s just gotten diagnosed is both simple and hard-won: “Cancer doesn’t define you. You define you. Even though you’re fighting for your life, help someone else fight for theirs.”.

In a recent development, charlotte Connor, 38, had just undergone a breast augmentation when she felt a lump in her breast. “When I saw my doctor, they weren’t concerned, in part because of my young age,” says Connor, who was 30 years old at the time. She had a mammogram and ultrasound to check for signs of cancer, but no MRI. “Looking back now I wish I would have asked for that MRI,” she says.

It has been revealed that at the first checkup six months later, they told her she was fine. At the second—one year after the original lump was found—the lump had tripled in size. Her doctor ordered a biopsy, and her diagnosis was confirmed: stage 2A ductal carcinoma, which means the cancer was growing but contained to the breast and surrounding lymph nodes.

Recent findings suggest that “When they told me I had cancer, I was calm,” she claims. Her mindset immediately shifted from a sinking feeling to being optimistic about the future. “I focused on getting healthy again,” says Connor, who started fantasizing about what she would do after treatment.

She remembers thinking, I may be feeling sick and throwing up from chemotherapy, but what restaurants am I going to go to after all this is over? It’s an outlook that didn’t necessarily come naturally to her, either. “I’m not even overly optimistic in life—I think I’m a realist—but in this situation, I shifted to being overly optimistic.”.

Part of that mindset shift was for her young daughter. “I couldn’t be pessimistic; I had to be strong for her,” she notes. “And I knew that how I acted in this situation was how she was going to mirror things and react to stressful situations when she got older.”.

Connor’s other pillar of support came from a tight-knit circle of friends and family, who threw her a head-shaving party before she lost her hair due to chemo. “Making things fun and lighthearted like that got me through my darkest, saddest moments,” she states.

It was 1999, and Donna Culmer had just received a clean mammogram. A few months later she felt a stone-size bump on her right side, so she went back to her ob-gyn to get it checked out. They redid the mammogram on both breasts, and while what she’d felt was actually a fibrocystic lump, the imaging found a small, not palpable spot on her left side that turned out to be a stage 1 cancer. “I was stunned,” Culmer says. “I didn’t even know what questions to ask.” She drove back to work in a daze and told her boss what had happened.

In a recent development, at 46 she was serving in the Navy as an instructor and trainer to personnel who were working alongside the Marines. She was married to a Marine and raising three children. There was no good moment for this. There never is.

It has been revealed that four months of chemotherapy followed, with nausea and exhaustion that never quite let up. Her doctors were concerned that the chemo might not work, so she had a mastectomy. Through it all her community refused to let her go through it alone. Her father drove her to every session and sat with her. Her church came to her, literally; services were held at her house.

According to recent reports, twenty-seven years later, Culmer, now 73, has had time to reflect. “As Black women, we have been through challenges our whole lives,” she notes. “This is just one more.” Her advice is practical and clear. “Don’t panic and ask questions, even if you have to write them down,” Culmer says. “The treatments available now are so much better than what I had.”.

One morning, Patricia Fox, 38, woke up with a lump in her right breast that wasn’t there the night before—she was just 26 years old at the time. Fox scheduled an appointment with her ob-gyn that day. “They told me that I was a young Black woman and had dense breasts, and it was likely a cyst,” she claims. “They were ready to turn me away.”.

The lump, which was a little smaller than a golf ball, seemed strange to Fox. Thankfully, she listened to her intuition. “There was something telling me to get it checked out,” she says, so her doctor did a biopsy just to be sure.

Her results came back as estrogen receptor-positive stage 2A breast cancer, meaning her cancer had estrogen receptors that would respond to hormone therapy drugs. Fox notes she’ll never forget her doctor’s words: “Patricia, you’ll be a breast cancer survivor.” That sentiment set the tone for her mindset as a fighter. “It made me think that I could face this and survive this,” she says.

Still, cancer treatments swiftly overwhelmed Fox, and soon she faced her lowest point: crying on the floor for hours, feeling like having cancer at such a young age was a punishment for being a “bad person.” But she pulled herself out of it with hard work in therapy.

“I found that talking to a therapist helped me process my diagnosis and examine the areas of my life—certain people and my own behavior patterns—that were cancerous for me that I needed to do something about,” she claims. “While therapy didn’t make the pain go away, it did make how I coped with it much better.”.

In the Black community, therapy is often taboo, notes Fox, but it’s become her mission to dispel that belief. “Therapy fortified me to get through cancer,” she says, “and I tell everyone that they don’t have to suffer in silence.”.

Annette Colden, 63, was sitting at her sister’s bedside during the last days of her final battle with breast cancer when the conversation turned to screenings. Her sister had been through cervical cancer and two bouts of breast cancer before passing away from the disease. “She made me promise I’d get my mammograms,” Colden notes.

Colden’s first two yearly mammograms were clear. On the third there was a spot, but she was told by her doctor that things looked okay and it wasn’t cancer—she just had lumpy breasts.

“There’s this inner feeling you have,” she indicates. “Something was inside me saying, That’s not right.” Her sister’s doctor had told her the exact same thing, but Colden was so happy to hear she didn’t have cancer that she didn’t follow up.

Industry observers note that A year later she went back for a mammogram, and that’s when her doctors found it: stage 0 breast cancer, meaning only abnormal cells had been found. She was 42. “Now, looking back, I always tell women that if something doesn’t feel right, get a second opinion.”.

Despite the diagnosis Colden remained calm. “I’m a religious person,” she says. “In my prayer I said, ‘Lord, if you will be my pilot on this journey, I’ll be your copilot.’” She immediately felt a sense of peace.

After her recovery she decided to share that calming presence with other women going through breast cancer at a support group through Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center, where she had treatment. “I say, ‘It’s going to be a long road. If you don’t want to travel it alone, I’m right there with you.’”.

In a recent development, and she means it. Sometimes that involves talking with someone at 3 a.m. when the pain from chemotherapy hits. Other times it means sending food delivery boxes to the homes of people with breast cancer who can’t muster the strength to leave. “My sister did a lot of support work before she got really sick,” she states. “This is her vision.”.

It has been revealed that ricki Fairley, 69, was in the security line at the airport for a work trip when she got a call from her doctor. They’d found a peanut-like lump under her nipple that turned out to be cancer.

Fairley, who was 55 at the time, said, “I don’t have time for this right now. I’ll call you when I get to my destination.” A couple days later she found out she had stage 3A TNBC, and it was really aggressive. Compared with other breast cancers, TNBC has fewer targeted-therapy treatment options, often spreads beyond the breasts, and is more likely to recur. Black women have nearly three times the risk of developing triple-negative breast cancer.

Her diagnosis woke her up. “It made me realize that I needed to get all of the ‘cancers’ out of my life,” Fairley says. During treatment that first year which involved a double mastectomy, aggressive chemotherapy, and radiation, she quit her job and started her own firm. Then she filed for divorce and later sold her house. “I quit my life and started a fresh one, and changed everything,” she says. “I had to learn that my peace is nonnegotiable. I really think that stress caused my breast cancer.”.

Sources indicate that A year later her life changed again. Fairley was diagnosed with metastatic breast cancer and told she had two years to live. After finding out her current doctor had only treated two previous cases of TNBC and both women had died in eight months, she found a newly introduced doctor, who was well-versed in current research and treatments for the disease. She beat cancer a second time. “I remember sitting at my daughter’s graduation thinking, Okay, I made it. What’s next for me?” Fairley claims. The answer: helping others. In the years that followed, Fairley cofounded The Black Breast Cancer Alliance, which works to reduce the mortality rate for Black women.

Picture this: you settle into a fully flat bed at 35,000 feet somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Champagne in hand, the city lights of New York fading behind you. In seven hours, you'll be in Paris. But right now, in this seat — a seat that costs upward of $6,000 in cash — you paid 53,000 points to be here. That's the Air France Business Class experience on the JFK–CDG route, and it's one of the most compelling premium cabin redemptions available to the ChooseFI community today. Let's talk about the math, because the math is what makes this a genuine FI moment. A round-trip business class ticket between New York and Paris on Air France routinely retails for $3,000 on the low end and climbs to $6,000 or beyond during peak travel periods. At 53,000 Flying Blue miles one-way, you're looking at a value of **5.7 to 11.3 cents per point** — in a world where most points are considered excellent at 1.5 to 2 cents. You are, quite literally, squeezing 3 to 7 times the average value out of every mile you've earned. The pricing inefficiency here is real and it's structural. Flying Blue's Promo Rewards program releases discounted award seats monthly, sometimes cutting standard pricing by 25–50%. When a Promo Reward surfaces on a transatlantic business class route, the gap between what you'd pay in cash and what you pay in miles becomes almost absurd. A $4,000 cash ticket redeemable for 53,000 points you transferred at no cost from your Chase Sapphire Reserve? That's **7.5 cents per point** — money that your future self will thank you for. Beyond the numbers is the *experience* itself. Air France's long-haul business class product on the Boeing 777-300ER features a fully flat bed in a 1-2-1 configuration, direct aisle access from every seat, genuine French hospitality, and a meal service that feels like a restaurant, not an afterthought. This isn't a product you suffer through — it's one you savor. For a community that builds wealth intentionally so they can live fully, this is exactly what travel rewards are designed to unlock: a world-class experience at a fraction of the cost, because you understood the system.

Monthly promotional pricing makes premium European travel consistently accessible.

Free calculator reveals when you could reach financial independence — plus a savings rate tracker, expense audit, and more.

The core mechanism here is Flying Blue's Promo Rewards program, and once you understand how it works, you'll never look at transatlantic business class the same way again.

Flying Blue is Air France-KLM's frequent flyer program and a member of the SkyTeam alliance. Unlike many loyalty programs that use a static award chart, Flying Blue uses dynamic pricing — meaning award costs fluctuate based on demand, route, and season. That sounds like a disadvantage, and for standard awards it often is. But Flying Blue offsets this with a monthly release of Promo Rewards: a curated list of routes where award seats are released at 25–50% below standard dynamic pricing, often with surcharges waived entirely.

This is the inefficiency. When Air France wants to stimulate demand on a specific route in a given month, it uses Promo Rewards to attract award bookings. The airline gets seats filled; you get business class to Paris for 53,000 miles instead of potentially 80,000+ at standard dynamic rates. It's a win-win — if you know to look for it.

Recent findings suggest that the transfer ecosystem is what makes this accessible. Flying Blue partners with every major transferable points currency at a 1:1 ratio:.

In a recent development, the practical implication: if you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred, Chase Sapphire Reserve, Amex Platinum, Amex Gold, Citi Strata Premier, Capital One Venture X, or Bilt Mastercard, you already have a direct pipeline to Flying Blue miles. Most transfers are instant, meaning you can spot a Promo Reward, confirm the seat exists, transfer points, and book — all in the same afternoon. That speed matters because Promo Reward seats can disappear promptly.

One nuance worth naming: fuel surcharges. On standard Flying Blue awards for Air France and KLM-operated flights, the program passes through carrier-imposed surcharges that can add $200–$500 to your redemption. However — and this is critical — Promo Reward bookings typically eliminate these surcharges, meaning you pay the miles cost plus only government taxes. Always confirm surcharge status before booking a non-Promo award.

Sources indicate that finally, understand the routing rules: Flying Blue allows open-jaw itineraries, meaning you can fly into Paris and home from Amsterdam (or vice versa), effectively building a multi-city European trip with a single award booking. The booking window opens 359 days in advance — proposal accordingly.

Head to FlyingBlue.com at the beginning of each month — Promo Rewards are typically released in the first week. Navigate to the "Promo Rewards" section under the Awards tab. You're looking for transatlantic routes in business class (referred to as "Business" or "La Première" on the site). Bookmark the page and set a calendar reminder. You can also follow ChooseFI community forums, frequent flyer blogs, and Flying Blue's social accounts, which announce Promo Rewards as they drop. When a JFK–CDG or similar North America–Europe business class Promo Reward appears at 53,000 miles, you're in the window.

Once you've identified a Promo Reward route, search for availability directly on FlyingBlue.com. Use the award search tool, select "Business" class, and enter your travel dates. Promo Reward seats are labeled distinctly in the results. If you see them, note the exact flight numbers, dates, and total miles required before doing anything else. Don't transfer points yet — just confirm the seats exist and are bookable.

In a recent development, initiate the transfer from your credit card rewards portal. Enter your Flying Blue membership number exactly as it appears on your account. For Chase and Amex, transfers post instantly — refresh your Flying Blue account and the miles should appear within minutes. For Capital One or Bilt, allow 1–2 days. For Marriott Bonvoy, note the 3:1 ratio (you'll need 159,000 Bonvoy points for 53,000 Flying Blue miles) and allow 1–5 days.

If Promo Reward seats aren't available on your dates, don't give up. Check standard award availability on Flying Blue — the pricing will be higher, but the experience is identical. Alternatively, set up alerts through third-party tools and revisit the search as your travel dates approach. Availability often opens closer to departure as airlines release unsold inventory.

It has been revealed that unlike most airline award programs that set a fixed or dynamic price and leave it, Flying Blue runs a monthly promotional cycle. At the beginning of each month, they release a list of routes with discounted award pricing. These Promo Rewards typically offer 25-40% off the standard mileage price and apply to both economy and business class. The discounted routes change every month, covering different destinations on a rotating basis. This means a route that is not on promotion this month may appear next month. The system rewards patience and monitoring: travelers who check the Promo Rewards page monthly and maintain transfer-ready points in Chase, Amex, or other programs can consistently find premium cabin deals to European destinations.

Let's walk through a real-world example that illustrates exactly why the ChooseFI community gets excited about this redemption.

Recent findings suggest that the Booking: You're flying JFK → CDG in Air France Business Class on a Boeing 777-300ER. It's a Tuesday evening departure — one of the best days for award availability — and you've snagged a Promo Reward seat at 53,000 Flying Blue miles plus approximately $65 in government taxes.

In a recent development, the Cash Alternative: A quick search on Google Flights reveals the same seat retailing for $4,200 on that date. That's not an anomaly — transatlantic business class averages $3,000–$6,000 depending on season and advance purchase. At $4,200 in cash versus 53,000 miles, you're extracting 7.9 cents per point in value. Your Chase Ultimate Rewards points just became extraordinarily potent.

It has been revealed that the Experience: You arrive at JFK and head to the Air France lounge before departure — accessible as a business class passenger. From the moment you board, the difference from economy is visceral. Your seat in the 1-2-1 configuration means no climbing over a stranger; you have direct aisle access. The seat fully reclines into a 180-degree flat bed with a thick mattress pad and proper bedding — not a glorified recliner, an actual bed. Breaking: Unlock Your Full Potential by Fixing These Common Triathlon Body Imbalances

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (973 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that triathletes can face muscle imbalances.
  • Triathlon training is all about repetition, with hours upon hours spent catching and pulling in the pool, turning the pedals on the bike, and turning the legs over on the run.
  • In a recent development, over time, these imbalances can impact performance directly or indirectly by contributing to injury development.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that triathletes can face muscle imbalances. These off-season exercises help build proper strength to prepare for next season. (Photo: Brad Kaminski/Triathlete).

Triathlon training is all about repetition, with hours upon hours spent catching and pulling in the pool, turning the pedals on the bike, and turning the legs over on the run. With that repetition comes natural imbalance, with some muscle groups getting overworked while others get neglected (or even weaken with age).

In a recent development, over time, these imbalances can impact performance directly or indirectly by contributing to injury development. That’s why taking time to identify and address these imbalances now will help keep you healthy in the long run.

According to recent reports, by pinpointing areas of weakness or asymmetry early on, athletes can target the stabilizing muscles, improve biomechanical efficiency across all three disciplines, and significantly reduce the risk of overuse injuries that often arise from repetitive strain. Here’s how.

While swimming is generally thought of as the “safest” discipline in triathlon, challenges can and do occur, often manifesting as “swimmer’s shoulder.” Swimmer’s shoulder is a bit of a catch-all term for pain in the front of the shoulder that encompasses several pathologies, including rotator cuff issues.

Industry observers note that typically, underlying laxity and instability exist. One factor that can contribute to shoulder problems is a strength imbalance between the shoulder internal and external rotators, with the internal rotators becoming disproportionately strong in comparison to the external rotators. This makes sense, as the shoulder internal rotators are active throughout the catch and pull, working to rotate the arm in and push against water.

Recent findings suggest that but the external rotators still play an key role, as they help to stabilize the shoulder joint, keeping the ball of the joint centered in the socket to help prevent impingement and pain with overhead use and shoulder abnormalities. To decrease injury risk, external rotators should have about two-thirds of the strength of the internal rotators.

Recent findings suggest that the most reliable, valid ways to check this involve specialized dynamometry equipment that measures force. But if you’re just looking to get a general idea, check how many reps of each of the below motions you can do until fatigue.

In this case, the test (lying prone, rotating the back of the arm up) can also be used as an effective strengthening exercise for external rotation. Start with higher reps, lower weights to learn the motion (3 sets of 10-12), then work up to higher weights, lower reps (4 sets of 6-8) to build more strength.

If this position causes pain or is too difficult at first, a side-lying shoulder external rotation is also a good option.

Sources indicate that while the incidence of overuse injuries attributed to cycling is generally lower than those attributed to running, they can and do occur, most commonly impacting the knee and lower back. Although singling out contributing factors is difficult, the prolonged posture and muscle activations associated with cycling predispose athletes to overdeveloped quadriceps and an undeveloped posterior chain (glutes, hamstrings, back extensors) and lateral hip muscles.

Cyclists need strong quads – these are the predominant muscle used to power the pedal stroke. But the glutes and hamstrings do assist, so neglecting those leaves some power on the table. Plus, that injury-prone lower back needs adequate strength and endurance to withstand hours spent in a forward-flexed position.

Also, because muscle weakness and tightness often go hand-in-hand, related limitations in mobility throughout the posterior chain limit a cyclist’s ability to comfortably hold more aggressive aero positions. Those quads of steel will only help so much if you’re sitting up to ease back and glute discomfort by the end of a long ride!

The strength and endurance of the posterior chain (and also the lateral hip, which can play a role when it comes to knee pain on the bike) can be checked using a single-leg bridge hold.

Sources indicate that the single-leg RDL is a good choice for eliciting both high force and stretch in the hamstrings and strengthening the gluteal muscles, back extensors, and lateral hips. Isolating each leg can also help with side-to-side imbalances.

When it comes to muscle strength and running, the glutes have been frequently implicated as the cause of (and solution to) many challenges. But, while the glutes do play an notable stability-related role in the run gait and deficits have been linked with injury, the true workhorse of the run gait – the calves – often gets overlooked and under-strengthened.

The soleus (one of the calf muscles) experiences forces of up to eight times body weight and produces up to 50% of forward propulsive power while running. Because the calves insert onto the heel via the Achilles tendon (which acts as a spring during running), the two are linked, with decreased calf strength seen in athletes with Achilles challenges compared to healthy controls.

In a recent development, strong calves can also help to protect against tibial bone stress injuries. Masters athletes lose calf strength (and Achilles tendon stiffness) disproportionately to other muscle groups with age, leading to both a reduction in propulsion and step length and an increased risk of lower leg soft tissue injuries such as strains and tendinopathies. So, when it comes to both performance and helping to guard against many common lower leg injuries, first check the powerhouse muscles below the knee!

Calf strength can be tested with a single-leg calf raise test.

The test here can again be used as the exercise – just load it up!

So, while the different disciplines and repeated motions of triathlon might lend athletes to certain imbalances, not all is lost! Triathletes can make themselves stronger, more resilient, and faster with some awareness and work – so don’t neglect those details.

#79989. Tech Report: How Triathlon and Incurable Cancer Have Given Me a Way to Live Despite My Diagnosis

Tech Report: How Triathlon and Incurable Cancer Have Given Me a Way to Live Despite My Diagnosis

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2005 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Age-group triathlete Rebecca Jaussi shares her personal story with Triathlete of how receiving a cancer diagnosis drove her to signing up for and racing an Ironman 70.3.
  • I have always believed that if I worked hard enough and planned carefully enough, I might chart the course of my life.
  • Running and occasional triathlons are at the top of my goal-making lists.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: FinisherPix Powered by Outside).

Age-group triathlete Rebecca Jaussi shares her personal story with Triathlete of how receiving a cancer diagnosis drove her to signing up for and racing an Ironman 70.3.

I have spent most of my life making looks.

Endless lists of goals. Race calendars. Career milestones. Bucket-list adventures. I have always believed that if I worked hard enough and planned carefully enough, I might chart the course of my life.

Running and occasional triathlons are at the top of my goal-making lists.

I was a late starter professionally, choosing to stay home with my children when they were young. When I eventually returned to school, I didn’t ease my way back in. I was accepted into an accelerated doctoral nursing program, completing an intense year of coursework and clinicals before becoming a registered nurse, followed by three years of doctoral study. In 2020, I earned my doctorate in nursing practice and became a family nurse practitioner.

I have always been willing to push myself, physically and mentally, and my tenacity has benefited me.

I never imagined I would need it to fight cancer.

Recent findings suggest that this story began with a fall. It was another beautiful morning on the North Shore of Oahu (where I was living at the time) in February 2023, and I was running a technical trail when I went down on a rocky section. I experienced a pop in my right hamstring and some pain. But I did what I always do and just kept going.

According to recent reports, I finished the run. I experienced some pain afterward, but not enough, in my mind, to stop running for good. I took a few days off and then returned to the trails.

As a healthcare provider, I knew better. But as a runner, I convinced myself otherwise.

In a recent development, I continued running through an increasingly persistent, insidious pain. Eventually, my pace deteriorated from slow to a limping shuffle. Finally, I went to my colleague who practiced sports medicine, and was referred to physical therapy.

Industry observers note that I started PT in May. My physical therapist told me I needed to stop running, and I thought that was an unreasonable course of action. There have been very few occasions in my life when I stopped running, including childbirth and surgery, and they were brief periods of time.

Running wasn’t simply exercise for me; it was where I found my flow state and truly part of my identity.

I didn’t feel ready or willing to give up running due to the pain but trusted my physical therapist, whom I considered a friend and a respected colleague, that this was the best course of action.

According to recent reports, for three months, I walked on flat trails. I continued my physical therapy exercises and cross-trained but abstained from running or hiking.

Sources indicate that when I returned for another assessment, my physical therapist was puzzled. I wasn’t improving. He suggested imaging, and that push changed everything.

I went in for an MRI of my right leg. The imaging was ordered for my mid-thigh, which was not where I had originally injured my hamstring. When I discussed this with the technician, I pointed out that it was in my hip region, so he modified the imaging order.

The MRI showed enlarged lymph nodes in my right groin, hip, and possibly behind my knee, which was an abnormal finding.

Industry observers note that I had no recent infection or other obvious explanation for the swollen lymph nodes. I asked colleagues and peers for their opinions, and most believed this was a benign finding.

Industry observers note that my mind vacillated between thinking that it was probably fine and the worst-case scenario of malignancy. It felt unsettling to me, and I decided to push for a biopsy rather than wait a few months for an ultrasound to see if the lymph nodes were still enlarged.

Sources indicate that after the biopsy, I waited eight grueling days for the results. The physician, who was also my colleague and friend, told me the findings indicated that I had a form of B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

According to recent reports, this was not easy to ingest, but I didn’t want to burden her with the heaviness of this diagnosis and began joking around. I was blasé and asked her, “How are we going to fix my leg so that I can run?” refusing to fall apart on the phone.

It has been revealed that then I hung up and broke down in front of my husband. Suddenly, all the prepares I had spent my life making seemed irrelevant. Questions revolved in my head. What would happen to my family? My future? My career?

Sources indicate that the next step I took was to do what I knew how to do, which was research my diagnosis to find out everything that I could about it. I wanted to know the prognosis, treatment options, statistics, anything to help me wrap my head around this.

What I discovered in this process was much more difficult to accept. There were things that I could not control.

I was driven to face the possibility that I may not live as long as I had expected. I had to accept that I would be living with the uncertainty of my health status and that fighting incurable cancer might become a permanent fixture in my life.

For someone who had devoted decades to building goals and marking off boxes, this was terrifying. There were no checklists for this.

I took time to process what I was facing and came to the recognition that I had a choice – not about living with cancer, but about living my life.

Most importantly, I still wanted to run.

Recent findings suggest that I was not going to allow this diagnosis to define me; I had a strong desire to live my life to the fullest with purpose and direction. I still wanted to work as a nurse practitioner for as long as I could. I still wanted to pursue medical humanitarian work. I still wanted to travel. I still wanted to be active.

In January, I was accepted into a clinical trial for immunotherapy.

Before treatment began, I did something that probably sounded slightly unreasonable to the people around me.

I signed up for Ironman 70.3 Hawaii on June 1, 2024.

Sources indicate that I asked my oncologist and the lead investigator of my clinical trial whether I could participate. They told me that I was the first patient they knew of to ask about competing in a half Ironman while undergoing treatment.

They gave me their blessing with one caveat: It would be essential to listen to my body. This was going to be physically taxing on my body due to the cancer already exhausting my body and undergoing treatment in addition to the rigors of training for a 70.3.

I understood the risks. I also understood something else: Training gave me a goal and purpose to keep moving.

Although cancer had taken away my perception of control, it hadn’t taken away my ability to choose a direction.

Industry observers note that I arrived in Kona on May 30, 2024. I was nervous and exhausted. I had received treatment the week before and was still recovering from it.

It has been revealed that my younger brother, who had agreed to race with me when I asked, and I gathered our swag and attended the informational session. As we were walking out, I saw the iconic walls of all the participants, their bib numbers, and the “why” wall. Seeing my “why” story on the wall solidified my resolve in what I was doing.

Sources indicate that the day before the race, I started receiving text messages with their pictures attached, early in the morning, from friends, family, and my whole care team from Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center, wearing a T-shirt that had my cancer ribbon with the words “Fight Cancer Like a Girl” on the front and “Team Rebecca 01” on the back. My amazing husband made nearly 100 shirts and sent them out, asking them to send me a picture and words of encouragement the day before the race. I felt so much love and support from the people in my life.

Recent findings suggest that on June 1, 2024, I stood on the beach waiting for my wave to start at Ironman 70.3 Hawaii. I remember feeling incredibly grateful to be there and have the ability to push my body to the limits.

Recent findings suggest that the race was hard; the winds were cranking so hard that several cyclists were blown into the lava rocks along the highway. It took some serious grit to keep going, but with my husband and kids driving by with my favorite songs blasting on the stereo, cheering me on, I was able to finish the bike.

It has been revealed that by the time I started the run, it was midday, and the sun was searing, with temperatures climbing above 90 degrees. My body was fatigued, and every part of me wanted the race to be done. I dug deep. My mantra was “I can do hard things” on repeat. I kept moving.

During those final miles, rolling thoughts in my head surfaced: If I can fight cancer, I can finish this race.

There was an alteration in my thinking and in the purpose of that day; this was no longer about the race but rather an understanding that I was capable of moving forward.

Industry observers note that I crossed the finish line with my brother beside me and my family waiting and cheering. I was overwhelmed by my emotions as I crossed the line.

My body was spent; however, there was something strangely beautiful about that exhaustion. I would rather be exhausted from swimming, cycling, and running than exhausted from lying still, consumed by the knowledge that I have incurable cancer.

My training looks different than it used to. Some days are hard, and my body needs downtime.

I’ve learned that listening to my body isn’t a weakness, or even optional at times, but rather a way for me to keep up the fight.

With every step I take, every mile I cycle, every lap that I swim, it is more than just training; it serves as a reminder that my body is still mine and truly a gift to be cherished.

My cancer diagnosis has altered my relationship with time. I functioned at a faster pace and was always thinking ahead about what was next: the next race, the next degree, the next goal, the next item to add to my list.

Sources indicate that I am more focused on the mile that I am in right now. I have not stopped making aims; I just hold them differently.

My desires to work, travel, race, and serve others remain, but their priority and intensity are more flexible, as my health and energy can be fluid.

This diagnosis has shifted my perspective – I no longer believe that my worth or value depends on completing every goal I write down.

Some days a win is simply to get out the door. Sometimes it is a slow swim, and the distance may be shorter than planned. Sometimes it is walking instead of running. Sometimes it is resting.

And sometimes, it is standing at a finish line I wasn’t sure I would ever reach.

It has been revealed that the trajectory of my life feels unsure and more constrained. However, I know that running, swimming, and cycling are things I can do at the moment, and they make me feel alive.

In a recent development, honestly, for me, that’s what endurance sport has become. This is not a means of escape from cancer but rather my way of living despite it.

One step, one mile, one breath, I will keep going.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Here’s the science, three ways to begin, and a client who started at 57 and is still going at 77.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People in their 70s, 80s, and 90s get meaningfully stronger when they start strength training, and beginners tend to see the biggest response to training.

You also need far less than you’d guess: 30 to 60 minutes of lifting spread across a week is a great starting point.

Here’s the science, three ways to begin, and a client who started at 57 and is still going at 77.

Sources indicate that A reader wrote me this week. Her whole email was one sentence:.

That hits deep. That fear of: have I missed my window?

I want to share with you what I shared with her, because the science behind this is actually super cool and empowering.

Your body doesn’t have a cutoff age.

People in their 70s, 80s, and 90s still get stronger when they start lifting. And it meaningfully improves how they move through their lives.

And if you’re someone who hasn’t trained before, or hasn’t trained in a while, I have even better news.

According to recent reports, as a beginner, your body is even more sensitive to training. Translation: you get even more reward for your effort!

In the first few weeks, most people feel stronger before they look any different.

That’s because a lot of early strength is actually your muscles and brain learning to coordinate. The movement gets smoother. Standing up from a chair feels a little easier. Etc.

Over a few months, muscle starts to build.

Your bones respond to the load too (strength training is one of the best-supported ways to support bone health as we age.).

You’ll start to feel some muscle in your arms that you didn’t notice there before, like this reader who’s been doing workouts 3x/week and kicking butt with it:.

Is every body different? Yes. Does it also depend on sleep, nutrition, and what else life is throwing at you? Also yes.

But the direction is the same for everyone. No matter your age, you can make a meaningful impact in your overall health, fitness, and quality of life!

1) Don’t start with workouts. Start with practice.

Take a few minutes each day to learn and practice a couple of strength moves.

You’re not training yet. You’re getting acquainted.

Recent findings suggest that try some push-ups off of the wall or the countertop. ​ Sit down in a chair, slow and controlled, and practice keeping your weight evenly spread across your feet (that’s a squat right there!).

Sources indicate that grab a gallon jug, some light dumbbells or canned goods or whatever you have on hand, and practice a one-arm row. See if you can feel it in your upper back as you pull the weight up.

Work within whatever your ability level is, what feels safe and approachable to start.

You’re collecting information about what your body is ready for, and learning exercises like you’re learning a new skill.

2) It takes way less than you think.

30-60 minutes of strength training in TOTAL across the week goes a surprisingly long way.

You can break that up however works best for you. A short 5-10min session most days of the week, inserting some “movement snacks” throughout the day, or a couple of longer sessions 2x/week, etc.

It doesn’t require hours of your day to make serious progress.

3) It’s easier to level up than to cut down.

Because your body is more sensitive to strength training, you’ll likely feel more sore in the beginning.

So in general, I recommend you err on the side of less is more.

In a recent development, if you do a few short sessions during the week, and wake up the next day feeling great with little to no soreness, great! You can add a bit more the next week.

Mentally, I’ve also just found it’s way easier to be “leveling up” than having to cut back, which really helps with building that early momentum.

Industry observers note that I couldn’t have remarked it any better myself, Becky. 😊.

No matter your age or where you’re starting from…YOU GOT THIS! 💪.

In a recent development, if you can’t get yourself to start a workout after a long day, the problem might not be the workout itself. It’s the gear shift from “couch” to “go.”.

A bridge task is a small, neutral action (not fun, not hard, just…meh) that you put in between the two so the jump is smaller.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the yin yoga pose we love to hate, Dragon Pose, is a smart recovery tool for cyclists to improve hip extension.
  • Sources indicate that the low torso angle on a tri-specific bike provides aerodynamic benefits, but also requires greater hip flexion.
  • Dragon Pose is useful for triathletes who spend a lot of time folded over the handlebars during indoor training through the winter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the yin yoga pose we love to hate, Dragon Pose, is a smart recovery tool for cyclists to improve hip extension. Because cycling involves repetitive hip flexion at the top of the pedal stroke, the primary hip flexor muscle (psoas major) can tighten and become compressed over time, making it harder to access a powerful position off the bike.

Sources indicate that the low torso angle on a tri-specific bike provides aerodynamic benefits, but also requires greater hip flexion. In the aero position, the hip flexors, which not only flex the hip but also stabilize the pelvis and lower back, repeatedly contract without fully extending, shortening the muscles and potentially leading to low back pain and stiffness.

Dragon Pose is useful for triathletes who spend a lot of time folded over the handlebars during indoor training through the winter. It can also help you during the warmer months by restoring hip extension and preparing you for the longer stride that running off the bike demands. On the run, you repeatedly load one leg as the hip extends behind the body. Dragon Pose simulates that position, so you step off the bike feeling ready to hit your running stride.

Add Dragon Pose to your recovery routine. Practice this pose after a training ride or race to stretch the hip flexors and improve hip mobility.

According to recent reports, keep in mind that multiple bike fit factors affect hip angle and comfort. This guide provides five elements of a proper bike fit for smoother pedaling and to keep your position within your comfortable hip flexion range.

Improving hip extension can help you feel less compressed on the bike, move more easily through transitions, and ease low-back discomfort.

#79985. Does Soreness Mean a Good Workout? No. Here’s What It Actually Tells You

📅 03 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (902 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nerdfitness ↗ Open Full Page

Does Soreness Mean a Good Workout? No. Here’s What It Actually Tells You

📅 03 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (902 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdfitness

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Soreness is not an indicator of a good workout, and not being sore doesn’t mean your workout didn’t count.
  • That day-after ache (DOMS) mostly tells you that you did something fresh, not something effective.
  • Progress is more reliably measured in your training log: more weight, more reps, more control over time, sore or not.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Soreness is not an indicator of a good workout, and not being sore doesn’t mean your workout didn’t count.

That day-after ache (DOMS) mostly tells you that you did something fresh, not something effective.

Progress is more reliably measured in your training log: more weight, more reps, more control over time, sore or not.

It has been revealed that rachael (a reader and all-around amazing person) sent me a question about this so well-organized it came with multiple choice answers. 😃.

I LOVE this question, because almost everyone who’s getting started (or starting again) wonders the same thing:.

According to recent reports, quick definition first. That achy, stiff, “why does it hurt to sit on the toilet” feeling that shows up a day or two after a workout has a name: DOMS, or Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness.

It usually peaks somewhere around 24-72 hours after you train.

Severe soreness is NOT an indicator of a good workout.

It’s a sign that you did something latest that your body isn’t used to yet:.

So it’s not something you need to chase.

But it’s also not something to be afraid of, especially if you switch up your routine and are mildly sore for a day or two.

Sources indicate that your body is adapting swiftly! And as you adjust to the new exercises, you’ll be less and less sore from it.

So when is soreness helpful, if ever? ​ Soreness can give us a useful signal that we worked a muscle we were trying to target and hadn’t felt before.

But if you’re SUPER sore? Like, can’t get out of bed the next day and have to waddle around like a newborn giraffe sore? That’s a sign the jump was bigger than your body needed.

And the real cost (beyond the discomfort) is that it gets in the way of your next couple of workouts. Either because your technique gets sloppy because everything hurts, or you’re so wrecked that you don’t want to show up at all.

The best way to lower your odds of severe DOMS is to ease into a fresh program slowly.

Start with fewer sets and lighter weights than you think you need, and build from there. 💪.

According to recent reports, yes! You DO need to push yourself over time in order to make progress:.

That’s the law of progressive overload, and there’s no getting around it.

Sometimes adding that extra bit will make you sore. Other times, it won’t.

Recent findings suggest that but it’s the underlying principle that matters: are you asking a little more of yourself over time? Not: did it hurt afterward?

So why do we care so much about soreness?

Here’s what I think we’ve fallen into with fitness in general.

We as humans operate really well with feedback. If we touch a hot stove, we get burned and know not to do that again.

We want to know, immediately after doing something, whether it worked or it didn’t.

And with strength training, you don’t feel stronger the next day. It takes time to build up.

So we reach for proxies that close that feedback loop.

It’s exactly like the story of minty toothpaste.

As the story goes, toothpaste manufacturers had a hard time selling their product until they added mint.

Suddenly, there was a tingly clean feeling you could latch onto. “Oh, this IS working.”.

Sources indicate that the mint doesn’t clean your teeth. But it’s associated with the thing that does, and it gave people something to feel.

That’s where soreness sits for me.

It’s not the REASON you’re getting stronger.

But it can be associated with the work you do, especially as a beginner who is new to exercise, so we’ve learned to chase the tingle.

✅ How much weight, how many reps, how many sets are you doing?

✅ Do you feel more stable and controlled with the exercise than you did last month?

Sources indicate that then great! It’s working. Doesn’t matter if you never get sore.

And if you do end up super sore after trying something new, it’s not that you “failed”.

Just take it as a cue to introduce things more gently next time. 😊.

So, back to Rachael’s multiple choice question.

C is really close. But I’ll add an fourth option:.

Sources indicate that D) Soreness tells you what was NEW. Your training log tells you what’s WORKING.

According to recent reports, no extra fitness points for being sore. No points off if you do end up sore, either.

All the points gently ramping things up over time, and showing up again next time. 🔥.

According to recent reports, is it bad if I’m never sore? No. If your weights, reps, or control are improving over time, your training is working, sore or not.

Industry observers note that how long does DOMS last? It usually peaks 24 to 72 hours after the workout and fades over a few days. If you’re regularly wrecked for longer, ease the jumps in your program.

According to recent reports, should I work out while sore? Mild soreness is fine to train through, and easy movement often helps. If you’re severely sore, target a different part of the body, scale down, or take another rest day; what we don’t want to do is have sloppy technique because we’re SO sore we can’t perform the exercise normally.

(Photo: Andrew Clark; Design in Canva).

Calin Van Paris is a YJ editor and certified yoga instructor. Here, she shares five yoga poses that can help you access gratitude throughout your body—just in case you’re having a tough time feeling it in your heart.

It has been revealed that the practice of gratitude can be a sticky subject. Certain events and times of year—season shifts, rites of passage, the holidays—prompt us to ponder the things in our lives that elicit gratitude. Life feels a little richer when experienced through the lens of gratitude.

It has been revealed that but at times, accessing that gratitude can be easier said than done. Global happenings and situations in our individual lives aren’t always sunny or sparkly, and we don’t always feel grateful. Sometimes we’re just mad, sad, frustrated, or over it—even in November and December.

Rather than convincing your head (or heart) to be thankful, try feeling it in your body first. The following yoga poses can help transform the sometimes elusive concept of gratitude into something more physical.

Industry observers note that spend a few minutes in one of these poses contemplating  gratitude. The rest of you might follow.

In a recent development, there’s something worshipful about bowing on your knees, which makes Child’s Pose (Balasana) an easy choice for this list. When you’re in a grateful state, thanking the Universe can become akin to a prayer or mantra, one worth saying over and over again. Spend some time here, with your forehead and palms pressed to the earth, and imagine roots sprouting from all points of contact.

Another shape that finds you close to the earth, Squat (Malasana) is a pose of both humility and strength. Your feet planted on the ground offer stability, while the deep squat requires the cooperation of your entire lower body. Add the usual prayer hands, and Malasana becomes a demonstration of gratitude for your body, spirit, and anything else you choose to be grateful for.

According to recent reports, when you imagine a full-body expression of joy, chances are the pose in your mind looks a lot like Upward Salute (Urdhva Hastasana). The act of standing strong and lifting your arms in celebration mirrors the instinctive expression of wholehearted gratitude. When you’re in an authentically grateful place, expressing it doesn’t feel like a chore or an obligation—it feels like a party.

Opening your heart can also begin in your body. Bending back in Camel Pose requires a certain amount of trust in your body as well as in gravity. Once you’ve found stillness in the pose, your heart and throat face upward in a way that’s both vulnerable and liberating. Embracing this shape is a physical prompt for you to revel in—and perhaps exude gratitude for—the human experience.

In a recent development, lying prone on your back is perhaps the ultimate shape of surrender. Savasana finds your front body fully exposed to the Universe and all it has to offer while your back body roots you to the earth. Stilling your mind and body here demands an acceptance of this present moment, just as it is. And if that isn’t an expression of gratitude, then perhaps nothing is.

Sources indicate that magnus Ditlev of Denmark wins the 2026 IRONMAN Florida in a World Record Time of 7:19:17 on November 7, 2026 in Panama City, Florida. (Photo by Donald Miralle/Getty Images for IRONMAN) (Photo: Getty Images for IRONMAN).

One month after a heartbreaking DNF in Kona, Magnus Ditlev (DEN) rode away from the field at Ironman Florida and never looked back. His 7:19:17 took 1:47 off the previous men’s iron-distance world best that Sam Laidlow (FRA) set at Challenge Roth earlier this year.

It has been revealed that florida was a chance at redemption for Ditlev, who had come agonizingly close to winning the Ironman World Championship in Kona. He’d taken the lead late on the bike and looked on course for the win until he abruptly came to a stop on the run with roughly 30 minutes of racing left.

Sources indicate that however, ahead of Kona, Ditlev said he was putting up career-best numbers across the swim, bike, and run at his training camp in Colorado. In Florida, he finally got to reap the rewards of what fitness could produce all the way to the finish line.

Ditlev came out of the water in fifth, right on the heels of Ben Kanute (USA) and Rudy von Berg (USA). He took his time in T1 and started the bike nearly a minute down, but it didn’t take him long to ride back to the front. And then, just past mile 10, he made his move. No one could go with him, and they wouldn’t be able to stay remotely close to him either.

By the time Ditlev came off the bike, he was 11 minutes clear of a chase group that included Sam Long (USA), von Berg, and Kanute. His 3:51:16 was the fastest bike split ever recorded at an Ironman, nearly two minutes quicker than the 3:53:12 Robert Kallin (SWE) rode at Ironman Kalmar in August.

Off the bike, he once again took his time in transition. But transitions were the only slow part of Ditlev’s day. Once through T2, he picked up another minute on the chasers over the opening 10 miles. He hit halfway in 1:15, on pace for a 2:30 marathon and well within reach of Laidlow’s 7:21:04. With such an unassailable lead, one can assume he must’ve known the record was within reach to keep such an aggressive pace.

Ditlev eventually closed with a 2:33:31 marathon, crossing the line in 7:19:17. Von Berg took second, 14 minutes back, securing the early Kona slot and podium he’d come for. Matt Hanson (USA), meanwhile, ran a remarkable 2:28:07 to beat Long to the final podium spot, but still finished 16 minutes behind Ditlev.

How Fast Do You Actually Lose Strength? Slower Than You Think

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You lose strength much more slowly than you probably think.
  • A few days off changes basically nothing, measurable losses take roughly two to four weeks depending on the quality (muscle endurance fades first, maximal strength last).
  • Muscle memory makes rebuilding faster than building the first time, and maintaining takes a fraction of the training that building did.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You lose strength much more slowly than you probably think.

A few days off changes basically nothing, measurable losses take roughly two to four weeks depending on the quality (muscle endurance fades first, maximal strength last).

Muscle memory makes rebuilding faster than building the first time, and maintaining takes a fraction of the training that building did.

Here’s the timeline, and how it can inform your training.

Has this question ever crossed your mind:.

This was an awesome question that Charles sent my way. (Thanks Charles! 🙌).

When life gets crazy and you find yourself skipping workouts, there’s a voice that says:.

I had that exact thought the first time I had to take significant time away for a back injury.

And heck, just recently my kiddos brought home the “crud” from school and I missed a full week of workouts.

So, let’s look at what actually happens, and what it means for your training.

Short version: a few days off doesn’t impact your maximum strength or muscle size basically at all.

Your muscles may look or feel “flatter”, but that’s because stored water and glycogen decrease, not because you are weaker.

Sources indicate that and this “pump” comes back promptly once you start training again. 💪.

Here’s a rough timeline of when we start to see the effects of detraining:.

Highly trained folks and older adults will notice detraining faster than upcoming or younger lifters (so they’ll sit towards the beginning of these timelines.).

But you don’t lose your progress in any meaningful way after a week or 2 away from the gym. 😊.

And if you DO have to spend significant time away for whatever reason, I have good news for you, too:.

“Muscle memory” is a real thing.

1) Your nervous system remembers how to do the movement.

The first session or two in the gym after time away may feel a bit clunky, but you’ll quickly regain the technique.

Recent findings suggest that and a big component of strength is neuromuscular coordination (i.e. your brain and muscles firing together more efficiently, which improves rapidly.).

2) The muscle itself seems to hold onto some of the machinery it built, so it rebuilds faster the second time.

A general rule of thumb is about 50% as long as you were away (so if you were away for 12 weeks, it may take ~6 weeks to rebuild your strength.) Take this with a grain of salt as there is a LOT of variation here. This isn’t a hard and fast rule.

(And you don’t want to jump right back in at 100%. Use the 50/50 rule to get yourself going again.).

The point is, it’s generally easier to rebuild than to build the first time.

The work you did before still counts.

Industry observers note that building muscle and strength? It takes time and effort.

No one wakes up a day after a workout and has just magically put on 5 pounds of muscle.

But maintaining what you’ve built?

That takes only a fraction of the volume.

Sources indicate that when you keep intensity the same (i.e. how hard the exercise is), doing 1/3 the number of sets maintains your strength for a loooong time. ​ The point being: doing ANYTHING during a period where you aren’t able to consistently work out is still really really helpful!

When life throws you off track with your fitness goals, you’re not starting back from square zero.

And even a single session each week with a couple challenging sets is enough to hold what you’ve built until things calm down.

There’s that old saying that: “The best time to invest was 20 years ago. The next best time to invest is today.”.

I think the same holds true for building up your fitness.

Every session you put in now is strength you get to keep later.
